A.q: How do macrolides interact with other drugs, and in what order of severity?
opts: They induce CYP3A, lowering substrate levels
The effect is inhibition through an inactive complex, not induction, and azithromycin is the weakest.
They chelate divalent cations, reducing absorption of co-administered drugs
Chelation is the tetracycline and fluoroquinolone interaction.
They displace substrates from plasma protein binding sites
Protein displacement is not the mechanism given.
Metabolites inactivate CYP3A, raising substrate levels
Correct. The ranking is the practical point: azithromycin is the one to reach for when interactions matter.

A.q: How does flucytosine achieve selectivity for fungal cells?
opts: It inhibits a fungal cytochrome P450 enzyme with no human counterpart
That is closer to the azole mechanism, and human cytochrome P450 enzymes do exist, which is why azoles interact with other drugs.
A fungal transporter pumps it in; human cells lack it
The lecture attributes selectivity to the converting enzyme, not to a transporter.
Cytosine deaminase converts it; human cells lack that enzyme
Correct. The missing human enzyme is the whole basis of selectivity.
It binds ergosterol, which human membranes do not contain
That selectivity argument belongs to the polyenes.

A.io: 10 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic agonists
A.q: Which vascular beds does dopamine dilate, and through which receptors?
opts: Renal and splanchnic, through dopaminergic receptors
Correct, which is distinct from its beta-one cardiac and high-dose alpha-one effects.
Coronary and cerebral, through beta-two receptors
Not the beds or receptors the lecture names.
Skeletal muscle beds, through alpha-two receptors
Alpha-two is presynaptic and central here.
Pulmonary vessels, through dopaminergic receptors
The lecture names renal and splanchnic arteries.

A.io: 2 — Common modes of action of antimicrobial agents
A.q: Azoles and allylamines both reduce ergosterol. At which enzyme does each act?
opts: Azoles inhibit 1,3-beta-D-glucan synthase; allylamines inhibit lanosterol demethylase
Glucan synthase is the echinocandin target and sits in the cell wall, not the ergosterol pathway.
Both inhibit lanosterol demethylase, differing only in binding site
They act at genuinely different enzymes in the pathway.
Azoles inhibit lanosterol demethylase; allylamines inhibit squalene epoxidase
Correct. Same pathway, different steps — which is why both end in decreased ergosterol.
Azoles inhibit squalene epoxidase; allylamines inhibit lanosterol demethylase
This swaps the two enzymes.

A.io: 7 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: cholinergic agonists
A.q: What are the two limits on pralidoxime?
opts: It works only in children, and only within one hour of exposure
Neither limit is given in the lecture.
It must be given orally, and it is inactivated by food
Route and food are not the stated limitations.
It reverses muscarinic but not nicotinic signs
The stated limits are central penetration and reversible inhibitors.
It does not enter the brain, and cannot overcome reversible inhibitors
Correct. It reactivates inhibited acetylcholinesterase but only within those limits.

A.io: 11 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic antagonists
A.q: What is propranolol used for beyond hypertension?
opts: Glaucoma, asthma and benign prostatic hyperplasia
Glaucoma belongs to timolol; asthma is a contraindication.
Shock, cardiac arrest and anaphylaxis
Those are adrenergic agonist indications.
Pheochromocytoma and clonidine withdrawal
Those are the alpha blockers.
Migraine, hyperthyroidism, angina and infarction
Correct, and after infarction it reduces infarct size and sudden death.

A.io: 10 — Outline appropriate patient education for dermatologic drugs
A.q: Which benzoyl peroxide effect must be raised before starting it?
opts: It can bleach hair, clothing and bedding
Correct. This is the practical warning that prevents a patient ruining clothes and abandoning the drug.
It causes a permanent blue-grey discolouration of the skin
The lecture describes bleaching and irritation, not permanent pigmentation.
It commonly causes systemic hypersensitivity reactions
The lecture lists skin and mucous membrane irritation rather than systemic reactions.
It stains the skin orange for the duration of therapy
Bleaching rather than staining is what the lecture describes.

A.q: Why is epinephrine added to a local anaesthetic?
opts: It speeds onset
The stated benefit is duration.
It reduces allergy
Not the reason.
It buffers the pH
Not the reason.
It prolongs the block
Vasoconstriction at the injection site.

A.q: Which allylamine is available both orally and topically, and which is topical only?
opts: Naftifine is oral and topical; terbinafine is topical only
This reverses the two agents.
Both are available only topically
Terbinafine is orally active.
Both are available only orally
Naftifine is a topical agent.
Terbinafine is oral and topical; naftifine is topical only
Correct. Both inhibit squalene epoxidase and are used for superficial dermatophyte infection.

A.q: Which antiviral approach does the acyclovir family represent?
opts: Inhibiting viral assembly
Assembly inhibition is listed separately from nucleic acid synthesis.
Inhibiting nucleic acid synthesis
Correct — the drug is incorporated into viral DNA and terminates the chain.
Inhibiting viral release
That is oseltamivir's approach.
Blocking uncoating after entry
Uncoating blockade is a listed approach but not this family's.

A.q: Why must renal function be watched during acyclovir therapy?
opts: It causes interstitial nephritis as a hypersensitivity reaction
Interstitial nephritis is listed among the aminopenicillin effects.
The drug crystallises in the renal tubule, so hydration must be maintained
Correct — a physical rather than a toxic mechanism of renal injury.
The drug is nephrotoxic through direct tubular necrosis
Direct tubular damage is amphotericin B's mechanism.
Its vehicle accumulates in renal impairment
That is voriconazole's cyclodextrin.

A.io: 1 — Recall the gross organization of the nervous system, sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions
A.q: How is the efferent division of the peripheral nervous system divided?
opts: Into the brain and the spinal cord, which together form the outflow
Brain and spinal cord are the central nervous system, not the efferent division.
Somatic, under voluntary control, and autonomic, under involuntary control
Correct. Afferent carries signals to the central nervous system; efferent carries them away and splits this way.
Into the afferent and enteric systems
Afferent is the other division of the peripheral nervous system entirely, not a branch of efferent.
Into the sympathetic and parasympathetic systems only, with no somatic component
Those two are subdivisions of the autonomic branch, and the somatic branch also exists.

A.q: Which electrolyte and renal effects accompany amphotericin B?
opts: Isolated hepatotoxicity with no renal involvement
Renal effects are the prominent ones for this agent.
Bone marrow suppression as the dose-limiting toxicity
Bone marrow suppression is the flucytosine concern.
Low potassium and magnesium, hypotension, renal tubule damage
Correct. The saline hydration is the practical countermeasure worth remembering.
High potassium and calcium with a rising filtration rate
The disturbances run in the opposite direction, and filtration falls rather than rises.

A.q: How do sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim block folate synthesis at two different steps?
opts: Sulfa at the PABA step, trimethoprim at the reductase
Correct. Two sequential steps in one pathway, which is what makes the combination synergistic.
Sulfa at the reductase, trimethoprim at the PABA step
This swaps the two enzymes.
Both inhibit dihydrofolate reductase, at different binding sites
They act at different steps of the pathway, not the same enzyme.
Sulfa blocks gut folate; trimethoprim blocks reabsorption
Neither acts on absorption or reabsorption; both inhibit synthesis enzymes.

A.q: Which azole enters the brain and treats cryptococcal meningitis?
opts: Caspofungin
Caspofungin is an echinocandin, not an azole.
Fluconazole
Correct. It also has the best oral absorption of the group and is excreted in the urine, which suits it to candidiasis.
Ketoconazole
Ketoconazole explicitly does not enter the central nervous system.
Itraconazole
Itraconazole's indications are blastomycosis, histoplasmosis and onychomycosis.

A.io: 10 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic agonists
A.q: What are epinephrine's emergency indications?
opts: Anaphylactic shock and cardiac arrest
Correct, alongside acute reversal of bronchospasm.
Cardiogenic and septic shock
Those are dopamine's indications.
Hypertensive emergency
That is intravenous labetalol.
Chronic heart failure
That is dobutamine's territory.

A.q: Ampicillin and amoxicillin are the drugs of choice for which set of indications?
opts: Enterococcus, Listeria, endocarditis prophylaxis and pneumonia
Correct. Aminopenicillins add some Gram-negative aerobic activity to the natural penicillin spectrum but still lack Staphylococcus coverage.
Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia and osteomyelitis
Vancomycin is the treatment of choice for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus in this lecture.
Pseudomonal, nosocomial and polymicrobial infection
Those are antipseudomonal penicillin indications, notably piperacillin/tazobactam.
Syphilis, gas gangrene, and meningococcal disease
Those belong to penicillin G, the natural penicillin.

A.q: What is the vancomycin loading dose in a critically ill patient?
opts: 15 to 20 milligrams per kilogram, rounded to the nearest 500 milligrams
That is the maintenance dose based on actual body weight, not the load.
7 milligrams per kilogram once daily
That is the tobramycin and gentamicin regimen.
1 gram regardless of weight
Vancomycin dosing in this lecture is weight-based.
25 to 30 milligrams per kilogram, rounded to the nearest 500 milligrams
Correct. The loading dose exists to reach the target trough quickly rather than waiting through several maintenance doses.

A.io: 10 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic agonists
A.q: Why is caution advised with dobutamine in atrial fibrillation?
opts: It depletes cardiac catecholamine stores
That is reserpine.
It increases atrioventricular conduction
Correct, which can accelerate the ventricular response.
It slows sinoatrial firing
It is a positive chronotrope.
It causes bronchoconstriction
That is a beta blocker effect.

A.q: Why is ketoconazole rarely used now?
opts: No CNS entry, and it inhibits CYP3A4
Correct, and itraconazole with its wider spectrum largely replaced it.
Intravenous only, with severe infusion reactions
Ketoconazole is oral, taken with meals, and also available topically.
It is the only azole ineffective against Candida
Its problems are penetration and interactions rather than a Candida gap.
It causes visual disturbance in about 30 percent of patients
That is voriconazole's characteristic effect.

A.io: 6 — Summarize the synthesis, release, and subsequent destiny of ANS neurotransmitters
A.q: From what is acetylcholine synthesised?
opts: Glutamate and glycine
Neither is a precursor of acetylcholine.
Tryptophan and serotonin
That is the serotonin pathway.
Acetyl coenzyme A and choline
Correct, and choline is recovered by recycling after the transmitter is degraded.
Tyrosine and dopamine
That is the adrenergic synthesis pathway.

A.io: 5 — Summarize side effects and toxic manifestations of dermatologic drugs
A.q: Which problem is specific to topical neomycin?
opts: It bleaches hair and clothing
That is benzoyl peroxide.
It causes hypopigmentation
That is azelaic acid.
It is inactivated by benzoyl peroxide
That interaction belongs to tretinoin.
It frequently causes sensitisation
Correct, and the class can also accumulate systemically.

A.io: 7 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: cholinergic agonists
A.q: What is another term for an indirect-acting cholinergic agonist?
opts: Anticholinesterase
Correct. They raise acetylcholine by blocking its degradation rather than binding the receptor.
Parasympatholytic
That is a cholinergic antagonist.
Antimuscarinic
That is also an antagonist term.
Choline ester
Those are direct-acting agonists such as bethanechol and carbachol.

A.q: What distinguishes a bacteriostatic drug from a bactericidal one?
opts: Bacteriostatic agents are given orally and bactericidal agents are given intravenously
Route is unrelated; penicillins are bactericidal and available orally, tetracyclines bacteriostatic and available intravenously.
Static halts growth; cidal disrupts enough to kill
Correct. The lecture's split is about whether the drug itself kills, not about how fast it works.
Static is Gram-positive only; cidal covers both
Spectrum and killing are independent properties; both categories in the lecture contain broad and narrow agents.
Static needs a higher concentration than cidal
Concentration matters for the pharmacodynamic classes, but it is not what separates static from cidal.

A.io: 5 — Summarize side effects and toxic manifestations of dermatologic drugs
A.q: Pustular inflammation on the trunk weeks after starting a steroid. What happens when it stops?
opts: No change, because the eruption is independent of the drug
The eruption is drug induced, and the lecture ties its course to withdrawal.
An initial worsening, because inflammation increases
Correct, and warning the patient of this in advance is what stops them abandoning the plan.
Immediate and complete resolution of the eruption
The lecture specifically describes an initial worsening rather than clean resolution.
Conversion of the pustules into open comedones
This transformation is not described.

A.io: 3 — Classify the neurotransmitters released and the types of receptors found within the ANS
A.q: What kind of agent is dopamine?
opts: Multiple functions by location, and usually inhibitory
Correct, which contrasts with acetylcholine being usually excitatory.
Purely excitatory, controlling muscle movement in spinal cord neurons
That is acetylcholine's description.
The major inhibitory transmitter of the brain
That is gamma-aminobutyric acid.
Involved chiefly in mood, appetite and sensory perception
That is serotonin.

A.q: A patient complains their pillowcases are going pale. Which agent?
opts: Benzoyl peroxide
It bleaches hair, clothes and fabric.
Tretinoin
Not a bleaching agent.
Clindamycin lotion
Not a bleaching agent.
Azelaic acid
Causes hypopigmentation of skin, not fabric.

A.io: 10 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic agonists
A.q: Why does a local anaesthetic solution often contain epinephrine?
opts: It provides additional analgesia of its own
The benefit described is vascular, not analgesic.
It prevents an allergic reaction to the anaesthetic
Not the reason the lecture gives.
It causes vasoconstriction at the injection site
Correct, and applied topically it also helps control capillary oozing.
It speeds systemic absorption of the anaesthetic
Vasoconstriction slows removal from the site rather than speeding absorption.

A.q: What is the dual mechanism of action of the fluoroquinolones?
opts: Inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV
Correct. The lecture notes the topoisomerase IV mechanism is poorly understood.
Inhibition of the 30S and 50S ribosomal subunits simultaneously
Fluoroquinolones do not act at the ribosome.
Sulfa at the reductase, trimethoprim upstream of it
That dual block is sulfamethoxazole with trimethoprim.
Inhibition of cell wall cross-linking and of beta-lactamase
Neither applies to this class.

A.q: A patient on clarithromycin has a rising digoxin level. What is the mechanism?
opts: Renal competition
Not the interaction described.
Protein displacement
Not the interaction described.
CYP3A4 inhibition
Macrolide metabolites form an inactive complex with CYP3A.
Cation chelation
That reduces absorption of tetracyclines and quinolones.

A.q: Which beta blocker is used topically for chronic open-angle glaucoma?
opts: Atenolol
A cardioselective oral agent.
Carvedilol
Oral, with added alpha-1 blockade.
Timolol
Reduces aqueous humour production.
Propranolol
Systemic, and contraindicated in asthma.

A.io: 7 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: cholinergic agonists
A.q: What is atropine's antisecretory use?
opts: Reducing gastric acid secretion in peptic ulcer disease
Not the use the lecture names.
Reducing bronchial secretions in asthma maintenance
The inhaled synthetic agents cover chronic obstructive pulmonary disease maintenance.
Preventing sweating in axillary hyperhidrosis
That is glycopyrronium.
Blocking respiratory tract secretions before surgery
Correct, and glycopyrrolate is used similarly before surgery.

A.io: 3 — Classify the neurotransmitters released and the types of receptors found within the ANS
A.q: What does norepinephrine act as?
opts: A hormone only, released from the adrenal cortex
It is a transmitter as well, and the adrenal medulla is the relevant gland.
An inhibitory transmitter in pain pathways of the spinal cord
That is serotonin.
Both a neurotransmitter and a hormone
Correct, and it also regulates normal brain processes, usually excitatory.
A neurotransmitter only, with no hormonal role
The lecture explicitly gives it both roles.

A.q: A patient in acute heart failure needs inotropic support. Which agent?
opts: Propranolol
Negative inotrope.
Dobutamine
Raises cardiac output without much rise in oxygen demand.
Phenylephrine
A pure vasoconstrictor.
Clonidine
Lowers sympathetic outflow.

A.io: 7 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: cholinergic agonists
A.q: Which poisoning does physostigmine treat?
opts: Overdose of a cholinesterase inhibitor insecticide
That is treated with atropine and pralidoxime; giving another anticholinesterase would worsen it.
Beta blocker overdose
Not an indication given in this lecture.
Opioid overdose
Not an indication given in this lecture.
Overdose of anticholinergic drugs such as atropine
Correct. It raises acetylcholine to compete with the blocking drug.

A.io: 2 — Describe the molecular mechanism of action of dermatologic drugs
A.q: What is mupirocin's mechanism?
opts: It binds bacterial transfer RNA, preventing protein synthesis
Correct, and the lecture notes it is not absorbed though it may irritate mucous membranes.
It prevents bacterial cell wall synthesis
That is bacitracin.
It interrupts the bacterial cytoplasmic membrane
That is polymyxin B.
It inhibits fungal ergosterol production and so prevents cell wall synthesis
That is the allylamines.

A.q: What is the defining clinical advantage of aztreonam?
opts: The broadest beta-lactam spectrum, including anaerobes
Aztreonam has only Gram-negative coverage, with no Gram-positive or anaerobic activity at all.
Oral bioavailability allowing outpatient completion of therapy
It is given intravenously, 1 to 2 grams every 8 hours.
Reliable central nervous system penetration for meningitis
Central nervous system penetration is highlighted for carbapenems and third generation cephalosporins.
No beta-lactam cross-reactivity; safe in true allergy
Correct. That property is what makes a monobactam worth having despite its narrow Gram-negative-only spectrum.

A.io: 5 — Summarize side effects and toxic manifestations of dermatologic drugs
A.q: Which is a LOCAL adverse effect of topical steroids, not a systemic one?
opts: Cataracts
Cataracts are listed as systemic, alongside glaucoma.
Growth retardation in children
This is a systemic effect in the lecture.
Skin atrophy
Correct. Local effects are skin atrophy, acne, rosacea and allergic dermatitis related to the vehicle.
Adrenal suppression
This is on the lecture's systemic list.

A.q: Which azole has the best oral absorption, and how is it eliminated?
opts: Fluconazole, excreted in the urine
Correct, and its urinary excretion is part of why a single dose treats vaginal candidiasis.
Ketoconazole, excreted in the bile
Ketoconazole must be taken with meals and is the most limited of the group.
Itraconazole, excreted unchanged in the faeces
Itraconazole is orally active with an active metabolite, but fluconazole is the one noted for best absorption.
Posaconazole, excreted by the lungs
No such elimination route is described.

A.io: 5 — Summarize side effects and toxic manifestations of dermatologic drugs
A.q: Which two problems follow intralesional steroid injection of a nodule?
opts: Systemic absorption leading to adrenal suppression, and local tissue atrophy
Correct. Both are consequences of injecting a steroid into the lesion.
Permanent hyperpigmentation and keloid formation
Neither is what the lecture lists for this route.
Bleaching of hair and clothing
That belongs to benzoyl peroxide.
Photosensitivity and severe sunburn
That belongs to the topical retinoids.

A.q: Why is tacrolimus ointment second line rather than first for atopic dermatitis?
opts: Possible cancer risk
Second line after topical steroids.
It is ineffective
It does reduce severity.
It causes atrophy
That is the steroid effect.
It cannot be used on the face
Not the stated reason.

A.io: 10 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic agonists
A.q: What distinguishes dobutamine from other sympathomimetics?
opts: It produces no tolerance with prolonged use
Tolerance may develop with prolonged use.
It barely raises myocardial oxygen demand
Correct, which matters in a failing heart.
It has no effect on atrioventricular conduction
It increases atrioventricular conduction, hence caution in atrial fibrillation.
It can be given orally
Route is not the distinguishing feature given.

A.q: What does acyclovir achieve if started within 24 hours of chickenpox?
opts: It cures the infection and prevents later reactivation as shingles
The lecture is explicit that it does not cure the infection.
It has no effect unless combined with valacyclovir
No such combination requirement is given.
It prevents transmission to contacts but does not alter the illness
The stated benefit is a shorter acute illness.
It shortens the acute illness but does not cure the infection
Correct — the virus is not eradicated, which is why reactivation as shingles remains possible later.

A.q: From what source is amphotericin B derived?
opts: Penicillium griseofulvum
That is the source of griseofulvin.
Bacillus polymyxa
That is the source of the polymyxins, which are antibacterial.
The soil bacterium Amycolatopsis orientalis
That organism produces vancomycin.
A soil Streptomycetaceae organism
Correct, which places it alongside several antibacterials in being a natural product of a soil microbe.

A.io: 10 — Outline appropriate patient education for dermatologic drugs
A.q: Most topical acne agents irritate. What does that cause, and how should you start?
opts: It is prevented entirely by using an alcoholic solution
The lecture suggests considering non-alcoholic solutions, which is the reverse.
Patients stop; start low and increase gradually
Correct. Anticipating the irritation is what keeps a patient on therapy.
It confirms the drug is working, so maintain the starting strength
The lecture treats irritation as a barrier to adherence, not as a marker of efficacy.
Switch straight to systemic therapy
Severity, not irritation, is what moves a patient to systemic therapy.

A.q: Which two antivirals are given intravenously as the parent compound?
opts: Valacyclovir and famciclovir, each with an intravenous prodrug
Those two are the oral prodrugs rather than intravenous parents.
Oseltamivir and acyclovir, neither having an oral form
Oseltamivir is oral only, and acyclovir is available orally.
Valganciclovir and valacyclovir, given intravenously in transplant patients
Both are oral prodrugs.
Penciclovir and ganciclovir, each with an oral prodrug available
Correct — famciclovir and valganciclovir respectively are the better-absorbed oral forms.

A.q: Which fluoroquinolone should not be used for a urinary tract infection?
opts: All are suitable
Moxifloxacin is explicitly excluded.
Moxifloxacin
The one that does not cover urinary tract infection.
Ciprofloxacin
Used for urinary tract infection.
Levofloxacin
Used for urinary tract infection.

A.q: Cefazolin and cephalexin are first generation cephalosporins. What is their activity profile?
opts: Activity restricted to atypical organisms such as Legionella and Mycoplasma
Atypical coverage is a property of macrolides, tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones.
Gram-positives without Enterococcus, some Gram-negative cover
Correct. The absence of Enterococcus coverage is a recurring theme across the whole cephalosporin class.
Gram-negatives including Pseudomonas, plus Enterococcus
That profile belongs to later generations and to specific antipseudomonal agents.
Broad coverage including anaerobes and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus
Anaerobic and methicillin-resistant coverage are not features of the first generation.

A.io: 10 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic agonists
A.q: What is phenylephrine used for?
opts: Hypertension and opiate withdrawal
That is clonidine.
Glaucoma
That is timolol or pilocarpine.
Nasal decongestant, eye redness and septic shock
Correct.
Asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
That is albuterol.

A.q: What should a patient be told about taking griseofulvin with food?
opts: Food has no effect on absorption
A high-fat meal specifically increases absorption.
It should be taken with an antacid to reduce gastric irritation
No such advice is given, and antacids interfere with other agents.
Absorption is increased by a high-fat meal, because the drug is very lipid soluble
Correct, and it is effective against numerous dermatophytes but not Candida, acting fungistatically.
It must be taken on an empty stomach, since food chelates and inactivates the drug
Chelation with food is the tetracycline and fluoroquinolone problem.

A.q: Why is influenza treatment framed around a season?
opts: Resistance disappears outside the season
Resistance is described as an increasing problem over time, not a seasonal one.
Renal dosing requirements change with the season
Renal adjustment is not seasonal.
Flu season runs roughly October to March, which is when the illness is circulating
Correct, and it frames when an influenza-like illness should raise suspicion in the first place.
The drug is only manufactured and distributed during those particular months
Nothing about supply is described.

A.q: A patient on warfarin is started on Bactrim. What happens to the INR?
opts: It becomes unmeasurable
Not a real outcome.
It rises significantly
Through CYP2C9 inhibition.
It falls
The interaction runs the other way.
It is unchanged
A significant interaction is flagged.

A.q: When should a vancomycin trough be drawn?
opts: Immediately before the second dose
Levels drawn that early do not reflect steady state.
At any point within the dosing interval, provided the exact time of the draw is recorded
That flexibility applies to random levels in unstable renal function, not to routine troughs.
15 to 30 minutes before the next scheduled dose, usually around the third or fourth dose
Correct. Drawing around the third or fourth dose is what makes the level reflect steady state.
30 minutes after the end of the infusion
That is when a peak is drawn, and peaks are specified for the aminoglycosides.

A.q: What route and dosing consideration apply to oseltamivir?
opts: Available intravenously only, with hepatic adjustment
It is an oral agent and the adjustment named is renal.
Available orally and intravenously, with no adjustment needed
It is oral only, and renal adjustment is required.
Available as an inhaled powder only
Inhaled administration is not described for this agent.
Available orally only, and requiring renal dose adjustment
Correct. Renal adjustment is a consideration rather than a dose to memorise.

A.io: 2 — Describe the molecular mechanism of action of dermatologic drugs
A.q: What does imiquimod do?
opts: It is converted to benzoic acid after crossing the stratum corneum
That is benzoyl peroxide.
Corrects keratinization, cuts bacteria and inflammation
That is a topical retinoid action.
Drives interferon alpha and tumour necrosis factor release
Correct. It is an immunomodulator rather than a directly cytotoxic agent.
It inhibits T cell, mast cell and keratinocyte activation
That is tacrolimus and pimecrolimus, which suppress rather than stimulate.

A.io: 4 — Predict the effects of adrenergic and cholinergic stimulation and inhibition on effector organs
A.q: Which adverse effect is specific to atracurium?
opts: Rebound tachycardia on withdrawal
Not an effect described for this class.
Histamine release, with a fall in blood pressure and flushing
Correct, and it was replaced by its isomer cisatracurium for having fewer adverse effects.
Malignant hyperthermia in susceptible people
That is succinylcholine with halothane.
Prolonged paralysis from pseudocholinesterase deficiency
That relates to succinylcholine's breakdown.

A.io: 3 — Identify indications for commonly used dermatologic drugs
A.q: Which retinoid is used for Kaposi sarcoma?
opts: Alitretinoin
Correct. Bexarotene is the one paired with T-cell lymphoma.
Bexarotene
Bexarotene is the retinoid the lecture links to T-cell lymphoma.
Tazarotene
Tazarotene is used for acne and psoriasis.
Adapalene
Adapalene is an acne agent notable for its stability.

A.q: Which azole penetrates the central nervous system for cryptococcal meningitis?
opts: Itraconazole
Not the agent named for meningitis.
Griseofulvin
An antidermatophyte, not for meningitis.
Fluconazole
Best oral absorption and it penetrates the CNS.
Ketoconazole
Does not enter the CNS.

A.io: 4 — Predict the effects of adrenergic and cholinergic stimulation and inhibition on effector organs
A.q: Why is tyramine dangerous in a patient taking a monoamine oxidase inhibitor?
opts: It blocks reuptake of norepinephrine at the terminal
That is cocaine's mechanism.
It is converted into amphetamine in the liver
No such conversion is described.
It directly stimulates alpha-one receptors
It acts indirectly, by displacing stored norepinephrine.
Monoamine oxidase normally destroys it in the gut
Correct, and it is found in fermented foods such as cheese and wine.

A.io: 10 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic agonists
A.q: What happens if oxymetazoline is used beyond three days?
opts: Nasal septal perforation
Not described in this lecture.
Rhinitis medicamentosa, or rebound congestion
Correct, and it is the practical reason for a hard stop on a decongestant spray.
Permanent loss of the sense of smell
Not an effect the lecture describes.
Systemic hypertension requiring treatment
Rebound congestion is the stated risk.

B.io: 3 — Identify indications for commonly used dermatologic drugs
B.q: A lesion is oozing, vesicular and crusting. Which vehicle suits it?
opts: The least drying end of the range
That end is paired with scaling, lichenification and xerosis, which is the opposite presentation.
The middle of the range, regardless of the lesion
The lecture matches the vehicle to the lesion rather than defaulting to the middle.
Vehicle choice is not linked to lesion morphology
The lecture explicitly links the two.
The drying end of the range
Correct. Oozing, vesiculation and crusting are matched to drying vehicles; scaling, lichenification and xerosis to the least drying.

B.q: What are the black box warnings for the polymyxins?
opts: Ototoxicity, red man syndrome, and phlebitis
Those are vancomycin concerns.
Nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity, and neuromuscular blockade
Correct. These are the only warnings the lecture labels explicitly as black box, which is why they are worth holding separately from ordinary adverse effects.
Tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, and central nervous system effects
Those are fluoroquinolone adverse effects and are not labelled black box in this deck.
Thrombocytopenia, serotonin syndrome, and hypertensive crisis
Those are linezolid concerns.

B.q: A patient with asthma is started on propranolol and becomes wheezy. Why?
opts: Muscarinic blockade
Not the mechanism.
Beta-1 blockade
Cardiac, not bronchial.
Beta-2 blockade
Contraindicated in asthma and COPD.
Alpha-1 blockade
Not the mechanism.

B.q: Itraconazole is useful in which infections?
opts: Zygomycete infection including Mucor and Rhizopus
Posaconazole is the azole named for the Zygomycetes.
Systemic aspergillosis as first-line therapy
Voriconazole took that role from amphotericin B.
Blastomycosis, histoplasmosis and onychomycosis
Correct. It has an active metabolite and a wider spectrum than the ketoconazole it replaced.
Cryptococcal meningitis and relapse prophylaxis
Those are fluconazole's indications, which follow from its central nervous system penetration.

B.q: Under drug factors, which organ-system toxicities are considered?
opts: Gastrointestinal, renal, hepatic, ocular, reproductive, immunologic
Ocular, reproductive and immunologic are not part of the lecture's toxicity list at this point.
Hematologic, renal, hepatic, endocrine, vascular, lymphatic
Endocrine, vascular and lymphatic do not appear in the drug-factors framework.
Gastrointestinal, integument, hematologic, central nervous system, hepatic, renal
Correct. Six systems, and they map onto the monitoring parameters repeated for individual classes later in the lecture.
Cardiac, pulmonary, endocrine, musculoskeletal, ocular, and dermatologic systems
The lecture's list is different; cardiac effects appear later for specific agents rather than in this framework.

B.io: 5 — Summarize side effects and toxic manifestations of dermatologic drugs
B.q: Occlusion increases efficacy. What is flagged alongside it?
opts: It raises the question of increased toxicity as well
Correct. The lecture pairs the efficacy gain with a query about toxicity rather than presenting it as free benefit.
It reliably shortens the required duration of therapy
Duration is not the trade-off the lecture raises.
It prevents the vehicle from exerting any therapeutic effect of its own
The lecture states a vehicle may be therapeutic in itself, independent of occlusion.
It makes regional variation in penetration irrelevant
Regional variation remains a separate major variable.

B.q: Which mycoses are subcutaneous?
opts: Aspergillosis, cryptococcosis and histoplasmosis
Those are systemic.
Oral and vaginal candidiasis
Those are surface infections of mucous membranes.
Chromomycosis, Pseudallescheriasis and Sporotrichosis
Correct — the middle tier, affecting skin layers rather than the surface or the internal organs.
Tinea pedis, tinea cruris and tinea corporis
Those are superficial dermatophyte infections.

B.io: 10 — Outline appropriate patient education for dermatologic drugs
B.q: Why does an oral corticosteroid course for atopic dermatitis need a taper?
opts: To avoid precipitating drug-induced acne
Drug-induced acne is discussed under acne and is not the reason for the taper here.
To allow the topical steroid to be started safely
No such sequencing requirement is described.
To reduce the risk of secondary infection
Treating secondary infection is a separate goal of therapy.
To prevent a flare-up
Correct. The taper protects against rebound rather than against withdrawal symptoms alone.

B.io: 3 — Classify the neurotransmitters released and the types of receptors found within the ANS
B.q: Which terms mean the same as cholinergic antagonists?
opts: Anticholinesterases and indirect-acting agents
Those are agonists, acting by raising acetylcholine.
Anticholinergics, parasympatholytics or antimuscarinics
Correct, while the agonists are cholinomimetics or parasympathomimetics.
Cholinomimetics and parasympathomimetics
Those are the agonist synonyms.
Sympatholytics and adrenergic blockers
Those belong to the adrenergic side.

B.io: 3 — Identify indications for commonly used dermatologic drugs
B.q: When is acne treated topically rather than systemically?
opts: Topical for adults, systemic for adolescents
Age is not the lecture's dividing line.
Topical for the face, systemic for the trunk
Site is not what determines the route here.
Topical for mild to moderate disease, systemic for moderate to severe
Correct. Severity is what moves a patient onto systemic therapy.
Topical for inflammatory disease, systemic for comedonal disease
This inverts it; comedonal disease is where topical retinoid therapy is first line.

B.q: Which set of antivirals are prodrugs?
opts: Valacyclovir, famciclovir, valganciclovir and oseltamivir
Correct. Improving oral absorption is a recurring design theme across the whole antiviral section.
Acyclovir, penciclovir, ganciclovir and zanamivir
Those are parent compounds rather than prodrugs.
Amphotericin B, caspofungin and griseofulvin
Those are antifungals, and none is described as a prodrug.
Metronidazole, linezolid and daptomycin
Those are antibacterials outside this objective.

B.io: 4 — Predict the effects of adrenergic and cholinergic stimulation and inhibition on effector organs
B.q: What happens when epinephrine is given to a patient on a beta blocker?
opts: There is no clinically important interaction
The lecture lists it among the significant interactions.
Alpha effects are left unopposed
Correct. Blocking the vasodilating beta side leaves only vasoconstriction.
Both alpha and beta effects are abolished
The beta receptors are blocked; alpha remains available.
The blood pressure falls sharply
Unopposed alpha activity raises it.

B.q: Which tinea infection is commonly called ringworm?
opts: Tinea pedis
Tinea pedis is athlete's foot.
Tinea cruris
Tinea cruris is jock itch, affecting the groin.
Tinea unguium
Tinea unguium is onychomycosis, affecting the nails.
Tinea corporis
Correct. Despite the name there is no worm involved; it describes the annular appearance on the body surface.

B.io: 10 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic agonists
B.q: Norepinephrine extravasates and the skin blanches. What is the treatment?
opts: Dantrolene
That treats malignant hyperthermia.
Pralidoxime
That reactivates acetylcholinesterase.
Phentolamine
Correct. An alpha blocker reverses the intense local vasoconstriction before the skin sloughs.
Atropine
Atropine addresses the vagal reflex, not local vasoconstriction.

B.io: 3 — Identify indications for commonly used dermatologic drugs
B.q: Which vehicle is the most drying, and which the least?
opts: Creams are the most drying and gels the least
Both sit in the middle of the range rather than at its ends.
Powders are the most drying and lotions the least
Powders are within the list but tinctures anchor the drying end.
Tinctures are the most drying and ointments the least
Correct. The list runs tinctures, wet dressings, lotions, gels, aerosols, powders, pastes, creams, foams, ointments.
Ointments are the most drying and tinctures the least
This reverses the lecture's range.

B.q: Which enzyme does each of acyclovir and oseltamivir depend on or target?
opts: Acyclovir needs thymidine kinase; oseltamivir hits neuraminidase
Correct — one uses a viral enzyme to switch itself on, the other shuts a viral enzyme off.
Acyclovir hits neuraminidase; oseltamivir needs thymidine kinase
This reverses the two enzymes.
Both depend on viral thymidine kinase for activation
Only the guanine analogues do.
Both target viral neuraminidase at different sites
Only oseltamivir targets neuraminidase.

B.io: 10 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic agonists
B.q: Why is a selective beta-two agonist preferred over epinephrine in chronic asthma?
opts: Greater potency at beta-two receptors
Duration, not potency, is the stated reason.
Oral availability
Albuterol is inhaled in this context.
Absence of any tremor
Tremor is in fact listed among albuterol's adverse effects.
Longer duration of action
Correct. Epinephrine reverses acute bronchospasm; albuterol covers chronic treatment.

B.q: Which manifestations does cytomegalovirus cause?
opts: Retinitis, oesophagitis and colitis
Correct, and they occur chiefly in transplant recipients and other immunocompromised patients.
Chickenpox and shingles
Those are varicella-zoster.
Cold sores and genital ulceration
Those are herpes simplex types 1 and 2.
Influenza-like illness with fever and myalgia
That is influenza, treated with oseltamivir.

B.io: 7 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: cholinergic agonists
B.q: What is carbachol used for, and what receptors does it hit?
opts: Lowering intraocular pressure in glaucoma
Correct, and it causes miosis and spasm of accommodation.
Stimulating an atonic bladder, with muscarinic activity only
That is bethanechol, which lacks nicotinic activity.
Treating xerostomia, with muscarinic activity only
That is pilocarpine.
Diagnosing myasthenia gravis, by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase
That is edrophonium, an indirect agent.

B.q: An immunocompromised patient needs prophylaxis against Pneumocystis pneumonia. Which drug?
opts: Doxycycline
Not the agent for Pneumocystis.
Metronidazole
Anaerobic cover, not Pneumocystis.
Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole
Treatment and prophylaxis for Pneumocystis jirovecii.
Azithromycin
Used for Mycobacterium avium prophylaxis.

B.io: 4 — Predict the effects of adrenergic and cholinergic stimulation and inhibition on effector organs
B.q: Why does cocaine exaggerate epinephrine's cardiovascular actions?
opts: It increases receptor synthesis
That mechanism is given for hyperthyroidism, not cocaine.
It inhibits monoamine oxidase
Cocaine is described as blocking reuptake rather than the enzyme.
It converts epinephrine to norepinephrine
No such conversion is described.
It prevents reuptake
Correct, so the transmitter persists at the receptor.

B.q: What must a patient starting metronidazole be counselled to avoid, and why?
opts: Dairy products, because of chelation reducing absorption
Chelation applies to tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones.
Tyramine-containing foods, because of hypertensive crisis
That caution belongs to linezolid.
Sun exposure, because of photosensitivity
Photosensitivity is a tetracycline and fluoroquinolone effect.
Ethanol, because of a disulfiram-like reaction
Correct. This is the class's signature counselling point, alongside headache, nausea and vomiting.

B.io: 1 — Identify dermatologic drug classes and commonly prescribed dermatologic drugs
B.q: Which antiandrogen is used for acne?
opts: Cyproterone
This agent is not on the lecture's list.
Spironolactone
Correct, and the lecture notes a gel formulation is available alongside oral use.
Finasteride
Finasteride is not the agent named in this lecture.
Ketoconazole
Ketoconazole appears here as a topical azole antifungal.

B.q: Which tetracycline precautions relate to children and pregnancy?
opts: Grey baby syndrome — avoid in all trimesters
That is a chloramphenicol effect and is not the caution given here.
Teeth discoloration and skeletal effects; avoid under 8
Correct. Both follow from the drug binding calcium in developing bone and teeth.
Cartilage damage — avoid under 18 years old
That caution belongs to the fluoroquinolones.
Kernicterus; avoid in the first 30 days of life
The neonatal restriction in this lecture attaches to ceftriaxone.

B.q: Which tinea infection is commonly called jock itch?
opts: Tinea corporis
Tinea corporis is ringworm of the body.
Tinea pedis
Tinea pedis is athlete's foot.
Tinea unguium
Tinea unguium affects the nails.
Tinea cruris
Correct, affecting the groin. The azoles are indicated across this whole tinea group.

B.q: Systemic aspergillosis unresponsive to itraconazole and amphotericin B. Which class?
opts: Echinocandins
Correct — their listed role is largely salvage, in refractory aspergillosis, oesophageal candidiasis, and febrile neutropenia not responding to antibiotics.
Polyenes
Amphotericin B is a polyene, and the question specifies it has already failed.
Allylamines
Allylamines treat superficial dermatophyte infection, not systemic aspergillosis.
Mitotic inhibitors
Griseofulvin treats dermatophytes and does not cover Aspergillus.

B.q: Which polyene is used specifically for oral candidiasis?
opts: Amphotericin B deoxycholate
That is the systemic intravenous agent.
Natamycin
Natamycin is named among the polyenes but the oral candidiasis agent specified is nystatin.
Caspofungin
Caspofungin is an echinocandin used for oesophageal candidiasis intravenously.
Nystatin
Correct, available as oral preparations and a topical powder, with systemic effects limited by poor absorption.

B.q: Which central nervous system effects are listed for acyclovir?
opts: Seizures, delirium and tremor
Correct, alongside nausea, vomiting, rash and bone marrow suppression.
Confusion, ataxia, seizures and coma
That fuller list belongs to ganciclovir and valganciclovir.
Peripheral neuropathy and tendon rupture
Those are fluoroquinolone effects.
Visual disturbance in about 30 percent of patients
That is voriconazole.

B.q: Which viruses does oseltamivir target, and in what season?
opts: Influenza A only, year-round
It targets both A and B, and the lecture gives a defined season.
Herpes simplex and varicella-zoster, circulating year-round
Those are the acyclovir family's targets.
Cytomegalovirus in transplant recipients
That is the ganciclovir indication.
Influenza A and B, in a season running roughly October to March
Correct, and resistance has been becoming a problem over time.

B.q: An aminopenicillin is added to warfarin. What is the interaction?
opts: Abnormal prolongation of the prothrombin time
Correct. The lecture lists anticoagulants first among the aminopenicillin interactions.
Reduced anticoagulant effect requiring an increased warfarin dose
The stated direction is prolongation, not reduction, of the prothrombin time.
No clinically meaningful interaction, since penicillins are renally cleared
The lecture explicitly lists an anticoagulant interaction for this class.
Increased risk of tendon rupture when the two are combined
Tendon rupture is a fluoroquinolone concern, and it is not a warfarin interaction.

B.io: 8 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: cholinergic antagonists
B.q: How does succinylcholine differ mechanistically from the nondepolarizing blockers?
opts: It competitively prevents acetylcholine from binding without activating the receptor
That is the nondepolarizing mechanism.
It inhibits acetylcholinesterase in the junction
That would be an indirect cholinergic agonist.
It blocks calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
That is dantrolene.
It depolarizes the junction like acetylcholine but is not rapidly destroyed
Correct. Continued binding leaves the receptor unable to transmit further impulses.

B.q: A patient on a monoamine oxidase inhibitor eats aged cheese and the pressure spikes. Why?
opts: Beta-2 stimulation
Not the mechanism.
Tyramine displaces norepinephrine
Normally destroyed by MAO in the gut.
Direct alpha agonism
Tyramine acts indirectly.
Cheese contains adrenaline
Not true.

B.q: What monitoring do the penicillinase-resistant penicillins need?
opts: Renal function alone, since the class is cleared entirely by the kidney
The stated dosing consideration for this class is hepatic function.
Serum drug troughs drawn before the fourth dose
Therapeutic drug monitoring with troughs applies to vancomycin and the aminoglycosides.
Creatine phosphokinase and muscle pain
Those are the daptomycin monitoring parameters.
Hepatic function, complete blood count, and signs or symptoms of anaphylaxis
Correct. Note the dosing consideration for this class is hepatic rather than renal function, unlike most other penicillins.

B.q: Herpes simplex meningitis. Which type affects the meninges?
opts: Type 2
Correct. Type 2 covers genitals, rectum, hands or meninges; type 1 covers mouth, face, skin, oesophagus or brain.
Type 1
Type 1 is associated with the brain rather than the meninges in this lecture's split.
Neither type; meningitis is a cytomegalovirus manifestation
Cytomegalovirus is associated with retinitis, oesophagitis and colitis.
Neither type; meningitis is caused by varicella-zoster only
Varicella-zoster causes chickenpox and shingles here.

B.io: 11 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic antagonists
B.q: In which patients is propranolol contraindicated?
opts: Those recovering from myocardial infarction
It is used after infarction to prevent a second event.
Those with asthma or chronic lung disease
Correct, because beta-two blockade causes bronchoconstriction.
Those with hypertension
Hypertension is one of its indications.
Those with migraine
Migraine prevention is an indication.

B.q: Which organisms is flucytosine indicated against?
opts: Helminths including roundworm and whipworm
Those are anthelmintic targets.
Cryptococcus neoformans and Candida
Correct, and it is given in combination rather than alone because resistance develops readily.
Dermatophytes of the nails and scalp
Those are treated by griseofulvin and the allylamines.
Aspergillus and the Zygomycetes
Those require voriconazole and posaconazole respectively.

B.io: 1 — Identify dermatologic drug classes and commonly prescribed dermatologic drugs
B.q: Which two properties distinguish adapalene from tretinoin?
opts: Adapalene is stable in sunlight and stable with benzoyl peroxide
Correct, and it also tends to be less irritating.
Adapalene is a systemic agent and requires pregnancy testing
Adapalene is a topical retinoid; the pregnancy programme belongs to isotretinoin.
Adapalene is used only for psoriasis rather than acne
Tazarotene is the retinoid the lecture links to both acne and psoriasis.
Adapalene must be applied only at night because it is photolabile
Photolability is the property the lecture assigns to tretinoin, and adapalene is the stable one.

B.q: A poorly controlled diabetic develops a fungal infection. Which predisposing category?
opts: Suppression of competing organisms
That refers to antibiotic exposure clearing the bacterial flora.
Metabolic abnormality
Correct — diabetes is the lecture's own example for that category.
Immunodeficiency
That category is illustrated by cancer, human immunodeficiency virus infection, organ transplant and chemotherapy.
Loss of barriers
That covers burns, surgery and catheters.

B.q: A patient on levofloxacin develops sudden posterior ankle pain. What is the concern?
opts: Septic arthritis
Not the drug effect being tested.
Gout
Not a fluoroquinolone effect.
Compartment syndrome
Not a fluoroquinolone effect.
Achilles tendon rupture
Tendonitis and tendon rupture are the class risk.

B.q: A 2-week-old has suspected sepsis. Which cephalosporin is preferred?
opts: Cefazolin
Not the agent named for neonatal sepsis.
Cefepime
Not the agent named for neonatal sepsis.
Cefotaxime
Ceftriaxone cannot be used in the first 30 days of life.
Ceftriaxone
Contraindicated in the first 30 days of life.

B.q: What is the polymyxin mechanism of action?
opts: A detergent action on the Gram-negative outer membrane
Correct, which is why the spectrum is broad Gram-negative coverage — the target only exists there.
Inhibition of 1,3-beta-D-glucan synthase in the cell wall
That is the echinocandin mechanism in fungi.
Binds 30S and blocks transfer RNA at the A site
That is the tetracycline mechanism.
Covalent inactivation of penicillin-binding proteins
That is the penicillin mechanism.

B.io: 4 — Predict the effects of adrenergic and cholinergic stimulation and inhibition on effector organs
B.q: What must a patient do after handling a scopolamine patch?
opts: Wash their hands thoroughly afterwards
Correct. It is a small instruction that prevents an alarming symptom.
Avoid showering for twenty-four hours so the patch adheres
Not an instruction the lecture gives.
Apply the patch to the same site each time to maintain levels
Site rotation is not discussed, and this is not the stated instruction.
Take an antihistamine alongside it to prevent sedation
Sedation is an expected effect at lower doses rather than something countered this way.

B.io: 3 — Classify the neurotransmitters released and the types of receptors found within the ANS
B.q: Where are alpha-one receptors found, against alpha-two?
opts: Both exclusively on the postsynaptic membrane
Alpha-two is presynaptic in the lecture's account.
Both exclusively within the central nervous system
They are peripheral receptors, though central actions exist.
Alpha-one postsynaptically, alpha-two presynaptically
Correct, and that presynaptic location is what makes an alpha-two agonist reduce sympathetic outflow.
Alpha-one presynaptically and alpha-two postsynaptically
This reverses the two.

B.q: A patient on gentamicin reports new ringing in the ears. Which toxicity is this?
opts: Retinal toxicity
That is voriconazole's visual effect.
Ototoxicity
Listed with nephrotoxicity for the class.
Neurotoxicity
Not the effect described.
Hepatotoxicity
Not an aminoglycoside effect.

B.io: 7 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: cholinergic agonists
B.q: Into which two groups do the direct-acting cholinergic agonists divide?
opts: Catecholamines and noncatecholamines
That division belongs to the adrenergic agonists.
Choline esters and naturally occurring alkaloids
Correct. The esters are synthetic apart from acetylcholine itself.
Reversible and irreversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitors
Those are the indirect-acting agents, which raise acetylcholine rather than binding the receptor.
Antimuscarinics and ganglionic blockers
Those are cholinergic antagonists.

B.io: 11 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic antagonists
B.q: Which effect do the alpha-adrenergic blocking agents share?
opts: Reduced aqueous humour production
That is timolol.
Reflex tachycardia
Correct, and their effects on blood pressure are more profound when the patient stands.
Reflex bradycardia
Falling blood pressure drives the rate up, not down.
Bronchoconstriction
That is a nonselective beta blocker effect.

B.q: Carbapenems are the drug of choice for which infections?
opts: Resistant Gram-negatives, ESBL producers, meningitis
Correct. Their resistance to hydrolysis by beta-lactamases is what makes them the answer to extended-spectrum producers.
MRSA bacteraemia, endocarditis and osteomyelitis
Carbapenem Gram-positive coverage explicitly excludes methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.
Uncomplicated urinary tract infection and outpatient sinusitis
Using a carbapenem for these would waste a reserve agent, and the lecture positions them for resistant organisms.
Atypical pneumonia caused by Mycoplasma or Legionella
Atypicals are covered by macrolides, tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones.

B.q: A young woman has septic shock after a retained tampon. Which antibiotic binds the toxin?
opts: Ceftriaxone
Not the toxin-binding agent.
Gentamicin
Not the toxin-binding agent.
Clindamycin
Used for toxin-mediated disease because it binds the toxin.
Vancomycin
Kills the organism but does not bind the toxin.

B.io: 5 — Identify the location and effects of alpha-one, alpha-two, beta-one and beta-two stimulation
B.q: At what dose does dopamine begin to cause vasoconstriction, and through which receptor?
opts: At low doses, through alpha-one
The lecture reserves vasoconstriction for very high doses.
At low doses, through beta-two
Beta-two is not the vasoconstricting receptor.
At any dose, through dopaminergic receptors
Dopaminergic activation dilates renal and splanchnic vessels.
At very high doses, through alpha-one
Correct, whereas its cardiac effect is beta-one and its renal effect dopaminergic.

B.q: What is amphotericin B's mechanism of action?
opts: Forms pores in ergosterol membranes, leaking ions
Correct. The drug is derived from a soil Streptomycetaceae, and the leak is why electrolyte disturbance is such a prominent toxicity.
It inhibits lanosterol demethylase, reducing ergosterol synthesis
That is the azole mechanism; amphotericin B binds ergosterol already present.
It inhibits 1,3-beta-D-glucan synthase, weakening the cell wall
That is the echinocandin mechanism.
A fungal enzyme converts it, then it blocks thymidylate synthase
That describes flucytosine.

B.io: 4 — Predict the effects of adrenergic and cholinergic stimulation and inhibition on effector organs
B.q: Which set matches atropine's adverse effects?
opts: Sedation, constipation and rebound hypertension
Those belong to clonidine.
Dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention and constipation
Correct, with bradycardia at lower doses and tachycardia at higher ones.
Salivation, lacrimation, diarrhoea and bronchospasm
Those are cholinergic agonist effects.
Fasciculations, weakness and hypertension
Those are nicotinic effects.

B.io: 8 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: cholinergic antagonists
B.q: What do ganglionic blockers do, and why are they rarely used?
opts: They act at the neuromuscular junction to relax skeletal muscle
That is the neuromuscular blocking agents.
They block alpha and beta receptors simultaneously
That describes labetalol and carvedilol among the adrenergic antagonists.
They block nicotinic receptors at sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia
Correct, and blocking everything at once is precisely why they are rarely used clinically.
They block muscarinic receptors only, sparing the sympathetic system
That is the antimuscarinic group.

B.q: Which electrolyte pattern accompanies amphotericin B?
opts: Low sodium alone
Not the listed pattern.
High calcium
Not the listed pattern.
Low potassium and low magnesium
Hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia.
High potassium and high magnesium
The opposite of the listed effect.

B.io: 11 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic antagonists
B.q: Which metabolic effect do the alpha-one blockers have?
opts: Raised low-density lipoprotein and triglycerides
That is propranolol.
Fasting hypoglycaemia
That is also propranolol.
No metabolic effect at all
The lecture credits them with an improvement.
Improved lipid profiles and glucose metabolism
Correct, which contrasts with propranolol's worsening of both.

B.q: A patient on imipenem with renal impairment has a seizure. Is this expected?
opts: Only with intrathecal use
Not the qualifier given.
Only in children
Not the qualifier given.
Yes, seizures are a known imipenem effect
The unique side effect flagged for this agent.
No, carbapenems do not cause seizures
Imipenem specifically does.

B.io: 3 — Identify indications for commonly used dermatologic drugs
B.q: Why is a sedating antihistamine advised for a child with atopic dermatitis?
opts: To treat the secondary skin infections
Treating secondary infection is a separate goal of therapy in the lecture.
To lower serum immunoglobulin E
No agent in the lecture is given for that purpose.
To reduce night-time itching
Correct. The sedating property is being used for the itch that disrupts sleep.
To reverse the skin barrier dysfunction
Barrier dysfunction is addressed by lubricants and hydration, not antihistamines.

B.io: 3 — Classify the neurotransmitters released and the types of receptors found within the ANS
B.q: How is the nicotinic receptor structured?
opts: An intracellular receptor that binds acetylcholine after it crosses the membrane
The receptor sits in the membrane as a channel.
Five subunits forming a ligand-gated ion channel opened by two acetylcholine molecules
Correct, and it is found in the central nervous system, adrenal medulla, autonomic ganglia and neuromuscular junction.
A seven-transmembrane receptor coupled to a G protein and a second messenger
That is the muscarinic receptor family's arrangement rather than the nicotinic one.
An enzyme-linked receptor that phosphorylates intracellular targets on binding
The lecture describes an ion channel.

B.io: 8 — Discuss potential drug-drug, drug-food, and drug-herb interactions
B.q: What is the interaction between benzoyl peroxide and tretinoin?
opts: The two together cause systemic hypervitaminosis A
No systemic vitamin A toxicity is described from this pairing.
Benzoyl peroxide inactivates tretinoin
Correct, and it is why adapalene, which is stable with benzoyl peroxide, is highlighted separately.
Benzoyl peroxide increases tretinoin absorption to toxic levels
The lecture describes inactivation, not enhanced absorption.
Tretinoin prevents benzoyl peroxide from converting to benzoic acid
The interaction runs the other way in the lecture.

B.io: 2 — Common modes of action of antimicrobial agents
B.q: Which antibiotic classes bind the 50S ribosomal subunit, and which bind the 30S?
opts: 50S: aminoglycosides, tetracyclines. 30S: macrolides, clindamycin
This reverses the two groups.
50S — fluoroquinolones, metronidazole; 30S — penicillins, cephalosporins
None of those four is a protein synthesis inhibitor; they act on DNA or the cell wall.
50S — vancomycin, daptomycin; 30S — linezolid, tigecycline
Vancomycin and daptomycin act at the cell wall and membrane rather than the ribosome.
50S: macrolides, clindamycin. 30S: aminoglycosides, tetracyclines
Correct. The bacterial ribosome is 70S against the mammalian 80S, which is the basis for selectivity.

B.io: 10 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic agonists
B.q: What are albuterol's adverse effects?
opts: Tremor, restlessness and anxiety
Correct, the familiar beta-two agonist profile.
Sedation, dry mouth and constipation
Those belong to clonidine and the antimuscarinics.
Bradycardia and bronchoconstriction
Those are beta blocker effects, the opposite direction.
Miosis, salivation and diarrhoea
Those are muscarinic agonist effects.

C.q: How does griseofulvin reach the site of a dermatophyte infection?
opts: It is concentrated in sebum and delivered through the sebaceous glands
The lecture describes deposition in keratin precursor cells.
It is actively transported across the dermis by macrophages
No such mechanism is described.
It is applied topically and penetrates the nail plate directly
Griseofulvin is given systemically; tolnaftate and naftifine are the topical agents.
It is deposited in keratin precursor cells in skin, hair and nails
Correct. That is why treatment lasts as long as the keratin takes to grow out.

C.q: A patient on metronidazole drinks alcohol and becomes flushed and nauseated. What is this?
opts: Alcohol withdrawal
The drug interaction is the point.
Serotonin syndrome
That belongs to linezolid.
Disulfiram-like reaction
The single most testable fact about this drug.
Anaphylaxis
Not the reaction described.

C.io: 3 — Identify indications for commonly used dermatologic drugs
C.q: Why is an azole sometimes combined with a corticosteroid?
opts: For more rapid symptom relief
Correct. The steroid addresses symptoms while the antifungal addresses the organism.
To prevent the development of resistance
Resistance is raised for erythromycin in acne, not as the reason for this combination.
To allow a shorter total course of therapy
The lecture still describes treatment as generally prolonged.
To make the preparation less irritating to the skin
Local irritation is listed as the adverse reaction, but symptom relief is the stated reason.

C.io: 11 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic antagonists
C.q: How is norepinephrine given?
opts: By inhalation
Inhalation is listed for epinephrine, not norepinephrine.
As a titrated intravenous infusion
Correct, which suits a drug used to support vascular resistance in shock.
As a single intramuscular injection
That route is listed for epinephrine.
Orally, in divided doses
Catecholamines are not effective orally.

C.q: A patient presents on day 4 of influenza. What limits oseltamivir?
opts: The 48-hour window for starting treatment has passed
Correct. Because the drug blocks release of new virus rather than clearing existing virus, starting late has little to act on.
Treatment should be started at a doubled dose to compensate
No dose escalation strategy is described, and dosing is not tested.
Treatment is equally effective at any point in the illness
The lecture is explicit that it must be started as soon as possible.
Acyclovir should be substituted
Acyclovir has no activity against influenza.

C.q: Which organisms cause the superficial mycoses of hair, nails and mucous membranes?
opts: Epidermophyton, Microsporum and Trichophyton
Correct. These are the dermatophytes that griseofulvin and the allylamines treat.
Aspergillus, Cryptococcus and Histoplasma
Those cause systemic mycoses of internal organs.
Chromomycosis, Pseudallescheriasis and Sporotrichosis
Those are subcutaneous, affecting the skin layers rather than hair and nails.
Candida, Coccidioides and Blastomyces
Those appear in the systemic group.

C.io: 2 — Common modes of action of antimicrobial agents
C.q: Which features of fungal cells explain why antibacterial antibiotics do not treat them?
opts: Prokaryotic: peptidoglycan wall, 70S ribosome
Fungi are eukaryotic; peptidoglycan and the 70S ribosome are bacterial features.
No cell wall at all, so wall agents have no target
Fungi do have a cell wall, of chitin, and the membrane sterol is ergosterol rather than cholesterol.
They replicate only inside host cells, so extracellular antibiotics never reach them
Obligate intracellular replication describes viruses, not fungi.
Eukaryotic: chitin wall, ergosterol membrane, nuclear membrane
Correct. Every antifungal class in this lecture exploits one of these differences, which is also why selectivity is harder than with bacteria.

C.q: Which vehicle gives the greatest potency for the same steroid?
opts: Foam
Not the ranking given.
Ointment
Ointment is greater than cream, which is greater than lotion.
Lotion
The least occlusive.
Cream
Intermediate.

C.q: What kind of compound is oseltamivir as administered?
opts: A monoclonal antibody against viral haemagglutinin
No antibody therapy is described here.
A live attenuated preparation
That would describe a vaccine rather than an antiviral drug.
A prodrug converted to its carboxylate form
Correct — another prodrug in a lecture full of them, alongside valacyclovir, famciclovir and valganciclovir.
An active guanine analogue requiring no conversion
It requires conversion, and it is not a guanine analogue.

C.io: 1 — Identify dermatologic drug classes and commonly prescribed dermatologic drugs
C.q: Which conditions make up the atopic triad?
opts: Acne vulgaris and rosacea
These belong to the acne section of the lecture.
Asthma and allergic rhino-conjunctivitis
Correct, and skin barrier dysfunction is what the lecture says plays the major role in the skin component.
Psoriasis and seborrhoeic dermatitis
Neither is part of the atopic triad as the lecture defines it.
Urticaria and angio-oedema
These are not the two conditions named.

C.q: Which group of five agents is bacteriostatic?
opts: Tetracyclines, clindamycin, aminoglycosides, metronidazole, trimethoprim
Aminoglycosides and metronidazole belong to the bactericidal list despite the others being correct.
Erythromycin, tetracyclines, sulfonamides, trimethoprim, clindamycin
Correct. These are the five the lecture places on the bacteriostatic side.
Penicillins, cephalosporins, aminoglycosides, vancomycin, metronidazole
Those five are the lecture's bactericidal list, not the bacteriostatic one.
Erythromycin, penicillins, sulfonamides, vancomycin, fluoroquinolones
This mixes the two lists; penicillins, vancomycin and fluoroquinolones are given as bactericidal.

C.io: 5 — Summarize side effects and toxic manifestations of dermatologic drugs
C.q: Which systemic corticosteroid does NOT cause drug-induced acne?
opts: Hydrocortisone
Correct. The lecture notes the eruption is not seen with hydrocortisone.
Prednisone
Prednisone is named elsewhere as an oral corticosteroid used in therapy, not as the exception here.
Dexamethasone
Dexamethasone is given as a treatment option, and is not the stated exception.
Methylprednisolone
This appears in the atopic dermatitis section, not as the exception.

C.q: Aminoglycosides are the drug of choice for which situations?
opts: Clostridium difficile colitis
That is treated with metronidazole or oral vancomycin.
Febrile neutropenia, sepsis, and enterococcal synergy
Correct, with Enterococcus covered only at synergy dosing rather than as monotherapy.
Community-acquired pneumonia and acute otitis media
Those are macrolide, aminopenicillin and respiratory fluoroquinolone indications.
Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus skin infection
Aminoglycoside activity is against Gram-negatives, not resistant Gram-positives.

C.q: Which patient should avoid topical tacrolimus or pimecrolimus?
opts: A patient using an emollient
Emollients are part of routine care and are not a conflict.
A patient with a weakened immune system
Correct, and the lecture pairs this with a possible cancer risk.
A patient with a history of acne
Acne is not a stated contraindication for these agents.
A patient over the age of sixty
Age alone is not given as a bar.

C.io: 7 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: cholinergic agonists
C.q: What is neostigmine used for?
opts: Treating an overdose of an anticholinergic drug
That is physostigmine, which enters the central nervous system.
Stimulating the bladder and gut, and reversing competitive blockade
Correct, and it can stimulate contractility before paralysing.
Diagnosing myasthenia gravis and assessing cholinesterase therapy
Those are edrophonium's roles.
Slowing the progression of Alzheimer disease
That is the donepezil group.

C.io: 4 — Predict the effects of adrenergic and cholinergic stimulation and inhibition on effector organs
C.q: Agitation, hallucinations, dilated pupils, dry flushed skin, fever, retention. Which toxidrome?
opts: Nicotinic, from ganglionic stimulation
That gives fasciculations and weakness with hypertension.
Beta blocker overdose
That would give bradycardia and bronchoconstriction rather than this picture.
Anticholinergic
Correct. The lecture gives it as mad as a hatter, blind as a bat, red as a beet, dry as a bone, hot as Hades, with retention and tachycardia.
Muscarinic, from a cholinergic agonist
That runs wet and slow: salivation, lacrimation, miosis and bradycardia.

C.io: 11 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic antagonists
C.q: What is timolol's ocular action, and what is it used for?
opts: It reduces aqueous humour production
Correct, a different route to lowering pressure than pilocarpine's.
It causes miosis, for chronic open-angle glaucoma
Miosis is the cholinergic agonist route.
It causes mydriasis, for examination of the fundus
That is an antimuscarinic effect.
It reduces corneal oedema, for keratitis
Not an action described.

C.q: Which two conditions does varicella-zoster virus cause?
opts: Retinitis and colitis
Those are cytomegalovirus manifestations.
Infectious mononucleosis and hepatitis
Neither is attributed to varicella-zoster here.
Chickenpox and shingles
Correct — primary infection and later reactivation of the same virus.
Cold sores and genital ulceration
Those are herpes simplex types 1 and 2.

C.q: Which pharmacokinetic properties count under drug factors?
opts: Bactericidal activity, time-dependent killing, and concentration-dependent killing
Those are pharmacodynamic properties, listed separately from pharmacokinetics on the same slide.
Absorption, distribution, penetration into body compartments, and elimination
Correct. Penetration into compartments is called out separately, which is why central nervous system penetration recurs for individual classes.
Onset, peak, duration, and half-life
Those terms are not the framework this slide uses.
Bioavailability, protein binding, volume of distribution, and clearance
Reasonable pharmacokinetic terms, but not the four the lecture lists here.

C.io: 4 — Predict the effects of adrenergic and cholinergic stimulation and inhibition on effector organs
C.q: What does nicotine do at autonomic ganglia?
opts: It has no ganglionic action and acts only in the central nervous system
It is the exception among ganglionic agents in the lecture.
It permanently destroys ganglionic receptors
The effect is depolarizing blockade rather than destruction.
It depolarizes the ganglia, first stimulating and then paralysing them
Correct, and the stimulation raises blood pressure, heart rate, peristalsis and secretions before the fall.
It competitively and reversibly blocks them from the outset
All the ganglionic blockers except nicotine are nondepolarizing competitive antagonists.

C.io: 10 — Outline appropriate patient education for dermatologic drugs
C.q: How well does ciclopirox nail lacquer work for onychomycosis?
opts: It is less than twelve per cent effective
Correct, and saying so up front is what keeps expectations honest for a months-long treatment.
It is curative in the majority of patients
The lecture reports a low success rate, not a majority.
It works only on fingernails, not toenails
The lecture markets it for both fingernails and toenails.
It is as effective as oral terbinafine
No such comparison is made, and the stated efficacy is low.

C.q: Which patient should not be given a topical retinoid?
opts: A patient taking an oral contraceptive
Oral contraceptives are listed as a useful acne therapy in some women, not a conflict.
A patient over sixty years of age
Age is not a contraindication, and the lecture notes retinoids are useful for wrinkles and dyspigmentation.
A patient who is pregnant
Correct. The lecture says to avoid retinoids during pregnancy.
A patient with a history of eczema
Eczema is not given as a contraindication to topical retinoid therapy.

C.q: Which Bactrim interaction runs through CYP2C9 inhibition?
opts: Chelation reducing absorption of iron supplements
Chelation belongs to tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones.
A significant increase in the international normalised ratio in patients on warfarin
Correct. Other interactions include raised phenytoin, rifampin and digoxin levels, reduced methotrexate clearance, and hypoglycaemia with sulfonylureas.
Reduced effectiveness of oral contraceptives through gut flora disruption
That is the aminopenicillin interaction.
Serotonin syndrome with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors
That is linezolid.

C.q: Which adverse reactions are listed for the echinocandins?
opts: Visual disturbance and hepatic dysfunction
Those belong to voriconazole.
Bone marrow suppression and hepatotoxicity as the principal dose-limiting effects
Those are flucytosine's effects.
Renal tubule damage requiring saline hydration
That is amphotericin B.
Tachycardia, headache, insomnia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and blood dyscrasias
Correct. Note the electrolyte disturbances overlap with amphotericin B's, despite a completely different mechanism.

C.q: Which of ganciclovir and valganciclovir is the better-absorbed oral form?
opts: Valganciclovir, the prodrug
Correct. Ganciclovir's oral bioavailability is very low, which is why the prodrug exists.
Ganciclovir, the parent compound
Ganciclovir is the poorly absorbed parent.
Both are equally absorbed
The prodrug is substantially better absorbed.
Neither is absorbed orally; both are intravenous only
Valganciclovir is an oral agent.

C.io: 4 — Predict the effects of adrenergic and cholinergic stimulation and inhibition on effector organs
C.q: Succinylcholine with halothane causes rigidity, acidosis, tachycardia and fever. What is the treatment?
opts: Pralidoxime to reactivate acetylcholinesterase
That is for anticholinesterase poisoning.
Atropine to oppose muscarinic overactivity
This is not a cholinergic crisis.
Neostigmine to reverse the blockade
Reversal is irrelevant to the hyperthermic reaction.
Rapid cooling and dantrolene
Correct, and blocking that release is what reduces heat production.

C.q: What is the approximate rate of penicillin cross-sensitivity with cephalosporins?
opts: Approximately 10 percent
Ten percent is a commonly repeated older figure, but the lecture gives a much lower one.
Approximately 25 percent
That would make cephalosporins largely unusable after a penicillin reaction, which is not the case.
Cross-sensitivity does not occur at all between the two classes
The lecture states cross-sensitivity exists, just at a low rate.
Less than 1 percent
Correct. The figure matters clinically because a reported penicillin allergy does not automatically exclude a cephalosporin.

C.io: 4 — Predict the effects of adrenergic and cholinergic stimulation and inhibition on effector organs
C.q: Why is propranolol hazardous for a patient prone to hypoglycaemia?
opts: It raises insulin secretion directly
Not a mechanism the lecture describes.
It increases glucose uptake into muscle
Not described here.
It blocks glucose absorption from the gut
Not described here.
It masks the response to hypoglycaemia
Correct, and it also decreases glycogenolysis and glucagon secretion.

C.q: Athlete's foot after prolonged occlusive footwear. Which predisposing factor?
opts: Loss of barriers
That covers burns, surgery and catheters breaching a physical boundary.
Immunodeficiency
That covers cancer, human immunodeficiency virus infection, transplant and chemotherapy.
Metabolic abnormality
That category is illustrated by diabetes.
A warm moist environment
Correct — the lecture's own examples for that category are diaper rash and athlete's foot.

C.q: A patient is hot, dry, flushed, confused, with dilated pupils and urinary retention. Which toxidrome?
opts: Sympathomimetic
Would sweat rather than be dry.
Opioid
Would give pinpoint pupils.
Anticholinergic
Mad as a hatter, blind as a bat, red as a beet, dry as a bone, hot as Hades.
Cholinergic
That gives salivation, lacrimation and diarrhoea.

C.q: What proportion of patients must stop intravenous ganciclovir because of side effects?
opts: About a third
Correct — a striking figure, and the reason the better-absorbed oral prodrug matters clinically.
About 1 in 20
The lecture gives a far higher proportion.
Almost none; it is generally well tolerated
It is poorly tolerated, which is the point of the slide.
Essentially all patients
The figure given is around a third rather than universal.

C.q: A 6-year-old needs an antibiotic. Why avoid doxycycline?
opts: Teeth discoloration
It binds calcium; also depresses skeletal growth.
Tendon rupture
That is the fluoroquinolone risk.
Seizures
That is imipenem.
Grey discolouration of skin
Not an effect this deck gives.

C.q: What distinguishes ceftriaxone from most other cephalosporins in renal impairment?
opts: It must be dialysed off before each subsequent dose
Nothing in the lecture supports this.
It requires no dosage adjustment in renal insufficiency
Correct, and it is a useful contrast because the class as a whole is mostly renally eliminated.
It requires the largest dose reduction of any cephalosporin in renal insufficiency
The opposite is stated — no adjustment is needed.
