It is contraindicated at any degree of renal impairment
No such contraindication is given; the caution attached to ceftriaxone concerns the first 30 days of life.

C.q: A patient stopped benzoyl peroxide because of irritation. What is the next step?
opts: Oral prednisone
Not the acne pathway.
Stop all treatment
Not a management step.
A topical retinoid
The next step he gave for this exact scenario.
Oral isotretinoin
Too large a jump for a first failure.

C.io: 5 — Identify the location and effects of alpha-one, alpha-two, beta-one and beta-two stimulation
C.q: Which receptor does phenylephrine act on, and what happens to the heart rate?
opts: Alpha-one, with reflex bradycardia
Correct. It has no direct cardiac action; the slowing is a baroreceptor reflex.
Beta-one, with tachycardia
That would be a direct cardiac stimulant such as dobutamine.
Beta-two, with no rate change
That is albuterol's receptor.
Alpha-two, with reduced sympathetic outflow
That is clonidine.

C.q: Which mood change must be monitored on isotretinoin?
opts: Mania
Not the flagged effect.
Psychosis
Not the flagged effect.
No monitoring is needed
Monitoring is explicitly required.
Developing depression
Explicitly flagged for monitoring.

C.q: A patient develops red man syndrome during a vancomycin infusion. What is the fix?
opts: Stop vancomycin permanently
The drug can be continued more slowly.
Give adrenaline
Reserved for true anaphylaxis.
Switch to oral vancomycin
Oral does not treat a systemic infection.
Slow the infusion
It is rate-related; the deck infuses 1 gram over 60 minutes.

C.io: 4 — Predict the effects of adrenergic and cholinergic stimulation and inhibition on effector organs
C.q: Which vascular effect does propranolol produce, and through which receptor?
opts: Renal vasodilation, through dopaminergic receptors
That is dopamine.
Peripheral vasoconstriction, through beta-two blockade
Correct, since blocking beta-two removes vasodilation.
Peripheral vasodilation, through alpha-one blockade
Propranolol does not affect alpha receptors.
No vascular effect at all
Vasoconstriction is listed among its actions.

C.q: Why does voriconazole's intravenous formulation require caution in renal failure?
opts: It crystallises in the renal tubule as acyclovir does
Tubular crystallisation is an acyclovir effect.
It causes direct renal tubule damage requiring saline hydration
That is amphotericin B's toxicity.
Its vehicle, cyclodextrin, accumulates when renal function is impaired
Correct — the concern is the vehicle rather than the drug itself, which is an unusual reason to avoid a formulation.
The drug itself is cleared entirely by glomerular filtration and reaches toxic levels
The stated problem is accumulation of the vehicle.

C.io: 6 — Summarize the synthesis, release, and subsequent destiny of ANS neurotransmitters
C.q: How do the indirect-acting cholinergic agents work?
opts: They bind muscarinic receptors directly and mimic acetylcholine
That is the direct-acting group.
They increase synthesis of acetylcholine from acetyl coenzyme A and choline
The lecture attributes their effect to blocking degradation, not to increasing synthesis.
They block reuptake of acetylcholine into the presynaptic terminal
Acetylcholine is degraded in the cleft rather than taken back up intact.
They increase the activity of acetylcholine by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase
Correct. They raise the transmitter rather than binding the receptor themselves.

C.io: 7 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: cholinergic agonists
C.q: Which antimuscarinic is approved for axillary hyperhidrosis?
opts: Glycopyrronium
Correct, approved in 2018 for that indication.
Dicyclomine
Dicyclomine is described as a structural analogue of atropine used for gastrointestinal spasm.
Tiotropium
Tiotropium is an inhaled bronchodilator.
Scopolamine
Scopolamine is used for motion sickness and secretions.

C.io: 11 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic antagonists
C.q: What happens to cardioselectivity at higher doses?
opts: It increases
The lecture states the opposite.
It is unchanged
Selectivity is dose dependent.
It converts to alpha blockade
No such conversion occurs.
It is lost
Correct, so a beta-one selective agent can still affect the airway.

C.io: 10 — Outline appropriate patient education for dermatologic drugs
C.q: What is the advice about washing in acne?
opts: Wash often with a high pH soap
A high pH may degrade the activity of other agents and is less tolerable on the skin.
Avoid washing the affected area entirely while on treatment
Cleansing is part of non-pharmacologic therapy rather than something to avoid.
Twice a day only, balancing cleanliness against drying
Correct, and it adds that once rinsed off no active product remains on the skin.
Wash as often as possible to remove surface oils
Excessive scrubbing and washing is listed as a contributory factor, so this would worsen the disease.

C.q: Which of the listed antiviral approaches works on the host rather than on the virus?
opts: Inhibiting viral protein synthesis
That acts on the virus.
Stimulating the host immune system
Correct — it is the only one of the eight aimed at the host side of the interaction.
Inhibiting specific viral enzymes
That acts on the virus.
Blocking viral assembly
That acts on the virus.

C.q: A woman is starting isotretinoin. Which programme must she enrol in?
opts: REMS for clozapine
The wrong programme.
A photosensitivity registry
Not a real requirement here.
No programme is needed
Enrolment is mandatory.
iPledge
Committed to pregnancy prevention.

C.io: 6 — Summarize the synthesis, release, and subsequent destiny of ANS neurotransmitters
C.q: How does guanethidine act?
opts: It blocks transport of transmitters into storage vesicles
That is reserpine.
It blocks postsynaptic alpha-one receptors
That is the prazosin group.
It stimulates presynaptic alpha-two receptors
That is clonidine.
It blocks release of stored norepinephrine
Correct, which is distinct from reserpine's blockade of vesicular uptake.

C.q: With which agents is flucytosine combined, and for what?
opts: With voriconazole in invasive aspergillosis, and with fluconazole in vaginal candidiasis
The stated combinations are with amphotericin B and with itraconazole.
With amphotericin in cryptococcal meningitis
Correct. It is used in combination rather than alone, and its own indications are Cryptococcus neoformans and Candida.
With caspofungin in oesophageal candidiasis, and with terbinafine in onychomycosis
Neither pairing appears in the lecture.
With griseofulvin in tinea capitis, and with nystatin in oral candidiasis
Those are dermatophyte and topical indications unrelated to flucytosine.

C.io: 1 — Identify dermatologic drug classes and commonly prescribed dermatologic drugs
C.q: Which set gives the MAJOR indicators of atopic dermatitis?
opts: Raised immunoglobulin E, positive allergy skin tests, and dry patchy scales
These are listed as minor indicators rather than major ones.
Nikolsky sign, mucosal erosion and a preceding fever
None of these belong to the lecture's atopic dermatitis criteria.
Comedones, papulopustular lesions, and nodules
These are acne lesions.
Pruritus, typical distribution, chronicity, family history
Correct. Raised immunoglobulin E, positive skin tests, dry patchy scales and infection susceptibility are the minor ones.

C.q: Why did aminoglycoside dosing move from every 8 hours to every 24 hours?
opts: Once-daily dosing eliminates the need for therapeutic drug monitoring
Monitoring is still required; peaks and troughs are specified around the third or fourth dose.
Renal clearance is so rapid that more frequent dosing has no effect
Renal toxicity, not rapid clearance, is the dosing consideration named.
Post-antibiotic effect and concentration-dependent killing
Correct. This is the clearest clinical application of the concentration-dependent pattern from earlier in the lecture.
Time-dependent killing over a longer interval
Time-dependent killing argues for frequent or continuous dosing, which is the opposite.

C.q: Voriconazole is derived from which other azole?
opts: Fluconazole
Correct — a fluconazole derivative introduced in 2002, which then took over systemic aspergillosis from amphotericin B.
Itraconazole
Posaconazole, not voriconazole, is the agent related to itraconazole.
Ketoconazole
Ketoconazole is the oldest of the group and is not voriconazole's parent.
Clotrimazole
Clotrimazole is a topical imidazole derivative.

C.q: Why is polymyxin resistance uncommon, and why is use expected to increase?
opts: It is used only topically, so systemic resistance cannot emerge
Route is not the explanation offered.
It is always combined with a beta-lactamase inhibitor that prevents resistance
No such combination is described.
Unused for 50 years; resistance is bringing it back
Correct. Low historical exposure is the reason resistance never developed widely.
Bacteria cannot circumvent it and the toxicity is gone
Proposed resistance mechanisms are listed, and the black box toxicities remain.

C.q: How is rebound congestion from oxymetazoline managed?
opts: Add an antihistamine
Not the stated fix.
Continue indefinitely
The three-day limit is the point.
Taper the drug down
A taper lets the receptors recover.
Increase the dose
Would deepen the rebound.

C.io: 1 — Recall the gross organization of the nervous system, sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions
C.q: Which three systems make up the autonomic division?
opts: Enteric, parasympathetic and sympathetic
Correct. The enteric system is the one most often forgotten of the three.
Somatic, parasympathetic and sympathetic
The somatic system is the other efferent branch, not part of the autonomic division.
Afferent, efferent and enteric
Afferent and efferent are the two divisions of the peripheral nervous system as a whole.
Central, peripheral and enteric
Central and peripheral are the two anatomical divisions of the nervous system overall.

C.io: 5 — Identify the location and effects of alpha-one, alpha-two, beta-one and beta-two stimulation
C.q: Where are adrenergic receptors located relative to the synapse?
opts: Presynaptically or postsynaptically
Correct, and that presynaptic location is what alpha-two agonists exploit.
Only postsynaptically on the effector organ
Alpha-two receptors sit presynaptically.
Only presynaptically on the neuron
Alpha-one and the beta receptors act postsynaptically.
Only within the central nervous system
They are found peripherally as well.

C.io: 8 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: cholinergic antagonists
C.q: Which three classes make up the cholinergic antagonists?
opts: Direct-acting agents, indirect-acting agents and reactivators
That framework belongs to the cholinergic agonists.
Alpha blockers, beta blockers and mixed blockers
Those are adrenergic antagonists.
Choline esters, alkaloids and anticholinesterases
Those are all agonist groups.
Antimuscarinic agents, ganglionic blockers and neuromuscular blocking agents
Correct, and they are distinguished by which cholinergic site they occupy.

C.q: Which infection is sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim used for in both treatment and prophylaxis?
opts: Lyme disease
Doxycycline is the tetracycline used for Lyme disease.
Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia
Correct, alongside urinary tract infection, bacterial prostatitis, orchitis and epididymitis.
Mycobacterium avium complex
That is treated with clarithromycin or azithromycin plus ethambutol.
Clostridium difficile colitis
That is metronidazole or oral vancomycin.

C.io: 4 — Predict the effects of adrenergic and cholinergic stimulation and inhibition on effector organs
C.q: Which cardiovascular effects does acetylcholine itself have?
opts: A rise in cardiac output with a fall in heart rate
Both fall in the lecture's account.
A decrease in heart rate, cardiac output and blood pressure
Correct, alongside increased salivary, intestinal and bronchiolar secretions.
An increase in heart rate with a rise in blood pressure
That is the nicotinic or adrenergic direction.
No cardiovascular effect, since its action is confined to glands
Cardiac slowing is one of its central actions.

C.q: Oral candidiasis after broad-spectrum antibiotics. Which predisposing factor?
opts: Metabolic abnormality
That category is illustrated by diabetes rather than by antibiotic exposure.
A warm and moist local environment
That category covers diaper rash and athlete's foot.
Suppression of competing organisms
Correct. Removing the bacterial flora leaves the niche open, which is why antibiotic exposure is itself a fungal risk factor.
Loss of barriers
Loss of barriers refers to burns, surgery and catheters breaching a physical boundary.

C.io: 5 — Identify the location and effects of alpha-one, alpha-two, beta-one and beta-two stimulation
C.q: Which receptors does isoproterenol predominantly stimulate?
opts: Beta-one and beta-two
Correct, which is why it heads the beta potency order and sits at the bottom of the alpha one.
Alpha-one and alpha-two
Those are phenoxybenzamine and phentolamine's targets as blockers.
Beta-one only
Dobutamine is the selective beta-one agent here.
Alpha-one only
That is phenylephrine.

C.io: 4 — Describe absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion of dermatologic drugs
C.q: A corticosteroid is not controlling a plaque. What does the concentration gradient predict?
opts: Changing to a more drying vehicle will matter more than concentration
Vehicle is a separate variable in the lecture; the concentration gradient is its own principle.
Only a change to a systemic agent will overcome it
Systemic therapy is reserved for moderate-severe disease, not for a single unresponsive plaque.
Raising the concentration increases drug transfer and can overcome the resistance
Correct. The lecture gives corticosteroid resistance overcome by increased concentration as its worked example.
Concentration has little effect once the stratum corneum is saturated
The lecture states the opposite: increased concentration means increased drug transfer.

D.io: 4 — Predict the effects of adrenergic and cholinergic stimulation and inhibition on effector organs
D.q: Which set matches the nicotinic effects?
opts: Sedation, hyperthermia, flushing, dry mouth and urinary retention
That is the anticholinergic toxidrome.
Vasodilation, atony of the bladder, cycloplegia and xerostomia
Those are the predominant effects of ganglionic blockade.
Mydriasis, tachycardia, weakness, hypertension and fasciculations
Correct, and note this set moves the pupil and heart in the opposite direction to the muscarinic set.
Miosis, bradycardia, bronchospasm, lacrimation and salivation
Those are the muscarinic effects.

D.q: A patient stops clonidine abruptly and the blood pressure spikes. What is this?
opts: Malignant hypertension of pregnancy
Not relevant.
Rebound hypertension
Never stop clonidine abruptly.
Pheochromocytoma
The drug history is the point.
Serotonin syndrome
Not the effect described.

D.q: Which organism does griseofulvin fail to cover, and what is the nature of its action?
opts: It is not effective against Candida, and it is fungistatic rather than fungicidal
Correct. It is effective against numerous dermatophytes, which is a different target population entirely.
It is not effective against dermatophytes, and it is fungicidal
Dermatophytes are precisely what it treats.
It is not effective against Aspergillus, and it is fungicidal against Candida
Its gap is Candida, and its action is fungistatic.
It covers all fungi but only when given topically
It is a systemic agent with a defined gap.

D.q: Which atypical organisms do macrolides cover?
opts: Rickettsiae, Borrelia burgdorferi and Brucella
Those animal-borne organisms are the tetracycline strength.
Legionella, Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila, Chlamydia
Correct, and this atypical coverage is what makes them a community-acquired pneumonia agent.
Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, Burkholderia, Stenotrophomonas
Those are resistant Gram-negative organisms outside the macrolide spectrum.
Bacteroides fragilis and Clostridium perfringens
The lecture states macrolides are not used clinically for anaerobes.

D.q: Which toxicities define the aminoglycoside class?
opts: Serotonin syndrome, hypertensive crisis, and thrombocytopenia
Those follow from linezolid's interactions.
Renal toxicity and ototoxicity, requiring renal dose adjustment
Correct, and vancomycin shares both, which is why the combination is watched carefully.
Hepatotoxicity and thrombocytopenia
Thrombocytopenia is the linezolid concern; hepatic effects belong to other agents.
Tendon rupture and peripheral neuropathy
Those are fluoroquinolone effects.

D.q: A patient with a true penicillin allergy needs gram-negative cover. Which agent is safe?
opts: Meropenem
A beta-lactam.
Piperacillin
A penicillin.
Aztreonam
No documented cross-reactivity with beta-lactams.
Ceftriaxone
A beta-lactam, though cross-reactivity is under 1%.

D.io: 3 — Identify indications for commonly used dermatologic drugs
D.q: Which agents are the gold standard for atopic dermatitis?
opts: Oral corticosteroids
These are used for short courses during exacerbations rather than as the standard.
Sedating antihistamines
These address night-time itching rather than the disease itself.
Topical corticosteroids
Correct, with the agent chosen by severity and by site of disease.
Topical immunomodulators
Tacrolimus and pimecrolimus are named as second line, after topical steroids.

D.io: 6 — Summarize the synthesis, release, and subsequent destiny of ANS neurotransmitters
D.q: Which sequence describes neurotransmission at a cholinergic neuron?
opts: Synthesis, storage, release, and inactivation by catechol-O-methyltransferase
That enzyme inactivates catecholamines, not acetylcholine.
Storage, release, binding, and permanent removal of choline from the neuron
Choline is recycled rather than lost.
Synthesis, storage, release, receptor binding, degradation, recycling of choline
Correct. Six sequential steps, and several drug classes act at one of them.
Synthesis, release, reuptake, repackaging
Reuptake of the intact transmitter is the adrenergic pattern; acetylcholine is degraded in the cleft.

D.q: Which organisms do tetracyclines cover excellently?
opts: Enterococcus and Listeria monocytogenes only
Enterococcus falls under good rather than excellent coverage, and the list is broader than this.
Anaerobes exclusively, with no aerobic activity
Anaerobes appear under good coverage, and the class is broad-spectrum.
Atypicals and animal-borne organisms
Correct. Poor coverage is specified for Pseudomonas and Clostridium difficile.
Pseudomonas, C. difficile, E. faecium, Acinetobacter
Those are named explicitly as poor coverage.

D.q: Which azoles are noted as teratogenic?
opts: Ketoconazole and posaconazole only
Teratogenicity is attributed to itraconazole, fluconazole and voriconazole in this deck.
None of the azoles carries a teratogenicity caution
Several do.
Only the topical imidazole derivatives
The topical agents are listed without that caution; the systemic ones carry it.
Itraconazole, and fluconazole and voriconazole in animals
Correct. Reproductive safety is a recurring caution across the azole group.

D.io: 5 — Identify the location and effects of alpha-one, alpha-two, beta-one and beta-two stimulation
D.q: Through which receptor does epinephrine produce bronchodilation?
opts: Alpha-two
Alpha-two is presynaptic and central here.
Beta-two
Correct, the same receptor albuterol targets selectively.
Beta-one
Beta-one is the cardiac receptor.
Alpha-one
Alpha-one mediates vasoconstriction and reduced insulin release.

D.q: What enzyme do the imidazoles and triazoles inhibit?
opts: Thymidylate synthase, blocking DNA synthesis
That is flucytosine's downstream effect.
Fungal cytochrome P450 14-alpha-demethylase, which converts lanosterol to ergosterol
Correct. Because the target is a cytochrome P450 enzyme, this class interferes with human cytochrome P450 enzymes too, which is the source of its drug interactions.
Squalene epoxidase, which acts early in the fungal ergosterol synthesis pathway
That is the allylamine target.
1,3-beta-D-glucan synthase in the cell wall
That is the echinocandin target.

D.io: 4 — Predict the effects of adrenergic and cholinergic stimulation and inhibition on effector organs
D.q: What are atropine's effects on the eye?
opts: Persistent mydriasis and cycloplegia
Correct, which is the opposite of the miosis and accommodation spasm the agonists cause.
Miosis with spasm of accommodation
That is the cholinergic agonist picture, carbachol and pilocarpine.
Reduced aqueous humour production with no change in pupil size
That is timolol.
No ocular effect at any dose
Ophthalmic dilation is one of its listed therapeutic uses.

D.q: A patient applies tretinoin each morning and burns. What is the advice?
opts: Apply it at night
Tretinoin is photolabile.
Apply it twice daily
Would worsen the irritation.
Add benzoyl peroxide
That inactivates tretinoin.
Stop all acne therapy
An unnecessary escalation.

D.io: 7 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: cholinergic agonists
D.q: What is pyridostigmine's clinical role?
opts: Diagnosis of myasthenia gravis
That is edrophonium.
Reactivating acetylcholinesterase after organophosphate exposure
That is pralidoxime.
Reducing intraocular pressure in glaucoma
Pilocarpine and carbachol are the ocular agents here.
Chronic management of myasthenia gravis
Correct, as distinct from edrophonium's diagnostic role.

D.q: Which central nervous system effects are listed for ganciclovir?
opts: Peripheral neuropathy and tendon injury
Those are fluoroquinolone effects.
Blurred vision and mental confusion from enzyme induction
That profile belongs to griseofulvin.
Confusion, ataxia, seizures and coma
Correct, occurring in a minority of patients alongside the haematologic effects.
Seizures, delirium and tremor only
That shorter list is acyclovir's.

D.q: Which adverse effects limit flucytosine?
opts: Tendon rupture and peripheral neuropathy
Those are fluoroquinolone effects and are not antifungal concerns.
Bone marrow suppression, hepatotoxicity, gastrointestinal disturbance and rash
Correct, and it is available orally only.
Nephrotoxicity and electrolyte wasting requiring hydration with normal saline
Those belong to amphotericin B.
Visual disturbance in about 30 percent of patients
That is the voriconazole effect.

D.io: 10 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic agonists
D.q: Besides blocking norepinephrine reuptake, what else does cocaine do?
opts: It inhibits monoamine oxidase
Not an action described for cocaine here.
It depletes vesicular stores of norepinephrine
That is reserpine and guanethidine.
It stimulates dopaminergic receptors in the kidney
That is dopamine's renal effect.
It blocks neuronal sodium channels
Correct, and it also blocks sodium-potassium activated ATPase.

D.q: Compared with acyclovir, what makes ganciclovir the harder drug to tolerate?
opts: Severe infusion reactions requiring premedication
Premedication for infusion reactions belongs to amphotericin B.
A disulfiram-like reaction on any alcohol exposure
That belongs to metronidazole.
Neutropenia and thrombocytopenia; a third stop treatment
Correct. Acyclovir's bone marrow suppression is listed, but ganciclovir's is far more limiting.
Crystals in the renal tubule; hydrate throughout
That is acyclovir's renal problem, not the reason ganciclovir is poorly tolerated.

D.q: Which infusion-related reaction is characteristic of vancomycin?
opts: Red man syndrome, along with fever, chills and phlebitis
Correct, and it sits alongside ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity among the monitoring concerns.
Disulfiram-like reaction when combined with ethanol
That is the metronidazole reaction.
Serotonin syndrome when combined with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor
That is the linezolid interaction.
Tendonitis and Achilles tendon rupture
That belongs to the fluoroquinolones.

D.io: 3 — Identify indications for commonly used dermatologic drugs
D.q: What is mupirocin used for beyond ordinary skin infection?
opts: Eliminating nasal carriage of Staphylococcus aureus
Correct, and its coverage is most gram positive aerobes, especially meticillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.
Eliminating vulvovaginal candidiasis in women
That indication belongs to the azole antifungals.
Treating recurrent orolabial herpes simplex
That is acyclovir and penciclovir.
Treating onychomycosis of the toenails
That is the ciclopirox nail lacquer.

D.q: Why are fever and chills expected during an amphotericin B infusion, and how are they managed?
opts: Fungal lysis releasing endotoxin, fixed by slowing the rate
Endotoxin release is not the mechanism described, and premedication is the stated management.
A disulfiram-like reaction to the vehicle
The disulfiram-like reaction belongs to metronidazole.
Interleukin-1 and tumour necrosis factor; pre-medicate
Correct. The reaction is a cytokine response rather than an allergy, which is why premedication works.
An IgE allergic reaction; stop the drug permanently
The mechanism given is cytokine-mediated, and the reaction is managed by premedication rather than by discontinuation.

D.io: 2 — Describe the molecular mechanism of action of dermatologic drugs
D.q: What are the two proposed actions of azelaic acid?
opts: Antimicrobial, and blocks testosterone conversion
Correct, and the lecture is explicit that the mechanism is not fully understood.
Inhibition of fungal cell wall formation and keratinolysis
Fungal cell wall inhibition belongs to the azole antifungals.
Converts to benzoic acid, with a comedolytic peeling effect
That is benzoyl peroxide's route.
Inhibition of T cell activation and mast cell stabilisation
That is the topical immunomodulator mechanism.

D.io: 1 — Recall the gross organization of the nervous system, sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions
D.q: What does the afferent division do, and what is an example?
opts: It controls gastrointestinal motility independently of the brain
That is the enteric system.
It carries signals to the central nervous system
Correct. The reflex arc needs the incoming limb before any autonomic outflow can be adjusted.
It carries signals away from the central nervous system to skeletal muscle
Carrying signals away is the efferent division.
It connects preganglionic to postganglionic neurons within a ganglion
That describes the efferent relay rather than the afferent division.

D.io: 4 — Predict the effects of adrenergic and cholinergic stimulation and inhibition on effector organs
D.q: Why give a small dose of a nondepolarizing blocker before succinylcholine?
opts: To allow a lower dose of anaesthetic agent
Reduced anaesthetic requirement is attributed to neuromuscular blockade generally.
To prevent the fasciculations that cause muscle soreness
Correct. It is a comfort measure that addresses a predictable adverse effect.
To prolong the duration of the block
That is not the stated purpose.
To prevent malignant hyperthermia
That risk is managed by avoiding the trigger and treating with dantrolene.

D.q: Three prodrug and parent pairs appear in the antiviral section. Which pairing is correct?
opts: Valacyclovir-ganciclovir, famciclovir-acyclovir, valganciclovir-penciclovir
The pairings are scrambled; each prodrug belongs to its own parent.
Oseltamivir-acyclovir, valacyclovir-penciclovir, famciclovir-ganciclovir
Oseltamivir is a prodrug of its own carboxylate form, unrelated to the guanine analogues.
There are no prodrugs among the antivirals in this lecture
Several are explicitly described as prodrugs.
Valacyclovir-acyclovir, famciclovir-penciclovir, valganciclovir-ganciclovir
Correct. In each case the prodrug exists to solve poor oral absorption of the parent.

D.q: What is the position on isotretinoin in pregnancy?
opts: Contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding; men too
Correct, and the iPledge programme exists around exactly this risk.
Safe after the first trimester
It is contraindicated, without a safe window.
It is contraindicated only in the first trimester
The lecture gives no trimester-limited allowance.
It requires no pregnancy precautions because it is applied topically
Isotretinoin here is the systemic retinoid, not a topical agent.

D.q: What is the collateral consequence of fluoroquinolone overuse?
opts: Permanent loss of Gram-positive coverage across the entire class
Resistance is described in general terms, not as a loss of Gram-positive activity specifically.
Cross-resistance to all beta-lactams
No such cross-resistance is claimed.
High rates of resistance, and Clostridium difficile as collateral damage
Correct. The slide states overuse equals resistance in capital letters, which is a deliberate emphasis.
Accelerated hepatic metabolism of co-administered drugs
Fluoroquinolones inhibit CYP1A2 rather than inducing metabolism.

D.q: What kind of infection are the allylamines used for?
opts: Superficial dermatophyte infections
Correct. Naftifine is topical and terbinafine is available orally and topically.
Systemic mycoses of the internal organs
Those require amphotericin B, the systemic azoles, or the echinocandins.
Cryptococcal meningitis
Fluconazole and amphotericin B with flucytosine are the agents for that.
Helminth infection
Those are treated by the benzimidazoles and pyrantel pamoate.

D.io: 1 — Identify dermatologic drug classes and commonly prescribed dermatologic drugs
D.q: How are acne lesions divided?
opts: Noninflammatory comedones; inflammatory papules and nodules
Correct. That split is what decides whether topical or systemic therapy is chosen.
Noninflammatory as papules; inflammatory as comedones
This reverses the two categories.
Superficial as pustular; deep as comedonal
The lecture divides by inflammation, not by depth.
Acute as nodules and pustules; chronic as comedones
The lecture treats acne as a chronic disease throughout rather than splitting it this way.

D.io: 5 — Summarize side effects and toxic manifestations of dermatologic drugs
D.q: Which laboratory change does isotretinoin cause?
opts: Reduced serum calcium
No calcium effect is described for isotretinoin.
Raised serum immunoglobulin E
Raised immunoglobulin E is a minor indicator of atopic dermatitis.
Reduced white cell count
Leukopenia is not on the lecture's list for this drug.
Increased serum lipids
Correct, and it sits alongside retinoid dermatitis, photophobia, arthralgia, headaches, alopecia and brittle nails.

D.io: 11 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic antagonists
D.q: What is intravenous labetalol used for?
opts: Septic shock
That is an adrenergic agonist indication.
Hypertensive emergencies
Correct, using its combined alpha and beta blockade.
Chronic open-angle glaucoma
That is timolol.
Acute asthma
A beta blocker would worsen bronchospasm.

D.io: 6 — Summarize the synthesis, release, and subsequent destiny of ANS neurotransmitters
D.q: How does reserpine act?
opts: It blocks transmitter uptake into vesicles
Correct, depleting norepinephrine, dopamine and serotonin.
It blocks release of stored norepinephrine from vesicles
That is guanethidine.
It blocks reuptake of norepinephrine at the terminal
That is cocaine.
It inhibits monoamine oxidase within the neuron
Reserpine works on vesicular transport, not the enzyme.

D.q: Which cephalosporin provides methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus coverage?
opts: Cefepime, a fourth generation agent
Cefepime explicitly lacks methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and Enterococcus coverage.
Ceftolozane/tazobactam, a fifth generation agent
This fifth generation combination also lacks methicillin-resistant coverage; its strength is antipseudomonal activity.
Ceftriaxone, a third generation agent
Ceftriaxone has good Streptococcus coverage but no methicillin-resistant activity.
Ceftaroline, a fifth generation agent
Correct. It is the cephalosporin that breaks the class's usual absence of methicillin-resistant coverage, and it must be renally adjusted.

D.q: A patient has used Afrin for a week and is more congested than before. What is this?
opts: Allergic rhinitis
The drug history is the point.
Sinusitis
Not the effect being tested.
Nasal polyps
Not a drug effect.
Rhinitis medicamentosa
Rebound congestion past three days.

D.q: Which non-neurologic adverse effects are listed for acyclovir?
opts: Neutropenia and thrombocytopenia as the dominant effects
Those are the ganciclovir effects.
Photosensitivity and tooth discoloration
Those are tetracycline effects.
Disulfiram-like reaction with ethanol
That belongs to metronidazole.
Nausea, vomiting, rash and bone marrow suppression
Correct, with hydration and renal function to be maintained because of tubular crystallisation.

D.io: 4 — Predict the effects of adrenergic and cholinergic stimulation and inhibition on effector organs
D.q: Which additional effect does carbachol produce through its nicotinic action?
opts: Depletion of stored norepinephrine
That is reserpine and guanethidine.
Release of epinephrine from the adrenal medulla
Correct, which is why its cardiovascular and gastrointestinal effects can be profound and biphasic.
Direct blockade of the neuromuscular junction
That is the neuromuscular blocking agents.
Inhibition of acetylcholinesterase
Carbachol binds the receptor directly rather than blocking the enzyme.

D.q: What happens to newly formed influenza virions when neuraminidase is inhibited?
opts: They can no longer attach to the receptor on the next host cell
Attachment is a separate step, and blocking it is a different listed approach.
They cannot uncoat once inside the next cell
Uncoating is another distinct approach in the list.
Their nucleic acid cannot be replicated
Nucleic acid inhibition is the guanine analogues' approach.
They cannot be cleaved free of the host cell as budding progeny
Correct — they remain tethered at the surface, so the infection cannot spread to new cells.

D.q: A patient asks how well ciclopirox nail lacquer works for onychomycosis. What do you say?
opts: Almost always curative
Overstates it substantially.
It works within two weeks
Not a duration claim the deck makes.
Under 12% effective
The figure the deck gives.
About half of patients
Overstates it substantially.

D.q: Which antiviral approach does oseltamivir represent?
opts: Inhibiting viral release
Correct — neuraminidase frees budding progeny, so blocking it traps new virus at the cell surface.
Blocking viral attachment to cells
Attachment blockade is a listed approach but not this drug's.
Inhibiting nucleic acid synthesis
That is the acyclovir family's approach.
Stimulating the host immune system
That approach is listed but is not oseltamivir's mechanism.

D.io: 4 — Predict the effects of adrenergic and cholinergic stimulation and inhibition on effector organs
D.q: What does nicotine do at the nicotinic receptor as concentration rises?
opts: It blocks the receptor at all concentrations
At low concentration it stimulates.
It has no effect on the nicotinic receptor, acting only at muscarinic sites
The receptor is named for nicotine's action on it.
It stimulates the receptor at low concentrations and blocks it at high concentrations
Correct, which is why nicotine appears in both the agonist and the ganglionic blocker discussions.
It stimulates the receptor at all concentrations, increasing with dose
The relationship reverses at high concentration.

D.q: What is metronidazole's mechanism of action?
opts: It inhibits dihydrofolate reductase
That is trimethoprim.
It interacts with bacterial DNA to cause loss of helical structure and strand breakage
Correct, and its activity spans Gram-positive and Gram-negative anaerobes plus parasites.
It inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV
That is the fluoroquinolone mechanism.
Binds 50S and blocks transpeptidation
That is the macrolide mechanism.

D.q: Twenty minutes into a vancomycin infusion a patient flushes red over the face and neck and itches. What is this?
opts: Stevens-Johnson syndrome
That is a mucocutaneous blistering reaction over days.
Serum sickness
That appears a week or more later with fever and arthralgia.
Red man syndrome
An infusion-rate reaction, not an allergy.
Anaphylaxis
That gives airway compromise and hypotension.

D.io: 4 — Predict the effects of adrenergic and cholinergic stimulation and inhibition on effector organs
D.q: Through which receptor does amphetamine raise blood pressure?
opts: Dopaminergic
Not the vascular route described.
Alpha-one
Correct, with beta-one accounting for the cardiac stimulation.
Beta-two
Beta-two would dilate rather than constrict.
Alpha-two
Alpha-two reduces sympathetic outflow.

D.q: A farm worker is bradycardic, salivating and wheezing after pesticide exposure. Which drug reverses the muscarinic effects?
opts: Pralidoxime
Reactivates the enzyme but does not enter the CNS.
Neostigmine
Would worsen it.
Physostigmine
Would worsen it.
Atropine
The antidote for cholinesterase inhibitor insecticides.

D.q: What distinguishes tolnaftate's spectrum from the other topical antifungals?
opts: Works on pedis, cruris and corporis, but not unguium
Correct. It works by distorting hyphae and stunting mycelial growth, and is topical only.
It is effective against tinea unguium of the nails but against none of the other tineas
The nail infection is precisely the one it does not treat.
It covers Candida but no dermatophytes
Its activity is against cutaneous mycoses, and Candida is not its target.
It covers systemic mycoses when given orally
It is available topically only.

D.io: 4 — Describe absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion of dermatologic drugs
D.q: What is the depot effect, and what does it allow?
opts: The vehicle evaporates and leaves crystals that dissolve slowly in sweat
This is not the mechanism given; the lecture attributes the effect to the skin as a reservoir.
Repeated applications saturate hair follicles and shut down absorption
The depot effect prolongs availability rather than stopping absorption.
Skin acts as a reservoir, allowing once daily dosing
Correct. The reservoir is what lets a short acting drug be given less often than its half-life suggests.
Stored in fat and released on exercise
The reservoir the lecture describes is the skin itself, not adipose tissue.

D.io: 11 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic antagonists
D.q: Which two alpha-one blockers are used for benign prostatic hyperplasia?
opts: Tamsulosin and alfuzosin
Correct, while prazosin, terazosin and doxazosin are listed for hypertension.
Prazosin and terazosin
Those are the hypertension agents.
Phentolamine and phenoxybenzamine
Those are the nonselective agents used for pheochromocytoma.
Labetalol and carvedilol
Those are mixed alpha and beta blockers.

D.q: Which macrolide-containing regimen is named for Helicobacter pylori?
opts: Azithromycin with doxycycline
That pairing is not the Helicobacter pylori regimen given here.
Erythromycin with metronidazole and omeprazole
The lecture names clarithromycin, amoxicillin and lansoprazole specifically.
Prevpac — clarithromycin, amoxicillin and lansoprazole
Correct. A macrolide, a penicillin and a proton pump inhibitor together.
Clarithromycin with ethambutol and rifabutin
That combination is for disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex.

D.q: A beta blocker begins with a letter from N to Z. What does that suggest?
opts: Cardioselective
That is A to M.
It has alpha blockade
That is labetalol and carvedilol.
It has intrinsic sympathomimetic activity
That is acebutolol and pindolol.
Non-selective
A to M are generally cardioselective.

D.q: How long does griseofulvin treatment take for scalp, fingernail and toenail infection?
opts: Scalp a week, fingernails a month, toenails three
These are far shorter than the durations given.
Three months for all three sites
The durations differ markedly by site.
A single dose for the scalp, with topical therapy thereafter for nails
Single-dose therapy is described for vaginal candidiasis with fluconazole, not here.
Scalp a month, fingernails 6 to 9, toenails up to 12
Correct. The gradient follows how slowly each keratin structure grows out, and it is the counselling point that keeps patients adherent.

D.q: Which are the three polyene agents?
opts: Caspofungin, micafungin and anidulafungin
Those are echinocandins.
Ketoconazole, miconazole and clotrimazole
Those are imidazoles.
Griseofulvin, terbinafine and naftifine
Griseofulvin is a mitotic inhibitor and the other two are allylamines.
Amphotericin B, nystatin and natamycin
Correct. Amphotericin B is the systemic agent; nystatin is used topically and orally because it is poorly absorbed.

D.io: 11 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic antagonists
D.q: Which of the two prevents cardiovascular mortality in heart failure?
opts: Pindolol
Pindolol is noted for intrinsic sympathomimetic activity.
Carvedilol
Correct, and it also decreases lipid peroxidation and vascular wall thickening.
Labetalol
Labetalol is the one given intravenously for hypertensive emergencies.
Propranolol
Propranolol's post-infarction benefit is described separately.

D.q: A patient presents on day 4 of influenza. What limits oseltamivir now?
opts: It is contraindicated in adults
It is not.
It must start within 48 hours
The window has passed.
It needs a negative rapid test
Not the stated limit.
It cannot be given orally
Oral is the only route.

D.io: 1 — Identify dermatologic drug classes and commonly prescribed dermatologic drugs
D.q: Which two agents are allylamines, and how do they work?
opts: Clotrimazole and miconazole, which inhibit fungal cytochrome P450
Those are azoles.
Nystatin and tolnaftate, binding membrane sterols
Those are grouped separately under other antifungals.
Ciclopirox and sertaconazole, which block precursor uptake
Ciclopirox blocks precursor uptake but is not an allylamine, and sertaconazole is an azole.
Naftifine and terbinafine, inhibiting ergosterol
Correct, with local irritation as the adverse reaction.

D.q: Which penicillin dosage form is given intramuscularly as a single long-acting dose?
opts: Penicillin G (benzylpenicillin)
Plain penicillin G is the intravenous form, dosed 18 to 24 million units daily in divided doses.
Ampicillin sodium
Ampicillin is an aminopenicillin given intravenously or orally, not a long-acting intramuscular depot.
Penicillin G benzathine (Bicillin)
Correct. The benzathine salt is the depot form, which is why one injection can cover an indication such as syphilis.
Penicillin V potassium (Pen VK)
Penicillin V potassium is the oral form, chosen because it is stable in stomach acid.

D.io: 7 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: cholinergic agonists
D.q: From which plants is atropine derived?
opts: Deadly nightshade, jimson weed and mandrake
Correct, and scopolamine comes from the same family.
Foxglove and lily of the valley
Those are sources of cardiac glycosides, not discussed here.
Opium poppy and coca
Cocaine appears later as an indirect adrenergic agonist, but not as a source of atropine.
Ephedra and willow bark
Ephedra relates to ephedrine among the mixed-action adrenergic agonists.

D.io: 2 — Describe the molecular mechanism of action of dermatologic drugs
D.q: What is the anti-inflammatory action of tetracyclines in acne?
opts: They stabilise mast cell membranes and block histamine release
Mast cell activation is addressed by the topical immunomodulators.
They inhibit the conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone
That is proposed for azelaic acid.
They stimulate macrophages to release tumour necrosis factor alpha
That is imiquimod's mechanism.
They chelate calcium ions, which prevents neutrophil and monocyte chemotaxis
Correct. That is an anti-inflammatory action separate from killing the organism.

D.io: 5 — Identify the location and effects of alpha-one, alpha-two, beta-one and beta-two stimulation
D.q: Which receptors does oxymetazoline act on?
opts: Dopaminergic
Those are dopamine's renal targets.
Alpha-one and alpha-two
Correct, producing vasoconstriction.
Beta-one and beta-two
Those are isoproterenol's.
Alpha-one only
Phenylephrine is the selective alpha-one agent.

D.io: 5 — Identify the location and effects of alpha-one, alpha-two, beta-one and beta-two stimulation
D.q: What is the rank order of potency at beta receptors?
opts: Isoproterenol, then epinephrine, then norepinephrine
Correct. The alpha order runs the other way, with epinephrine and norepinephrine far above isoproterenol.
Epinephrine, then norepinephrine, then isoproterenol
That is the alpha receptor order.
Norepinephrine, then epinephrine, then isoproterenol
This is not the order given for either family.
All three are equipotent at beta receptors
The lecture gives a clear rank order.

E.q: An 82-year-old on ciprofloxacin becomes confused and cannot sleep. What is the likely cause?
opts: Serotonin syndrome
That is the linezolid interaction.
Anticholinergic delirium
Not a fluoroquinolone effect.
Central nervous system toxicity
Dizziness, insomnia and somnolence, worse in the elderly.
Hepatic encephalopathy
Not the effect being tested.

E.io: 8 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: cholinergic antagonists
E.q: How are the neuromuscular blocking drugs described structurally?
opts: Structural analogues of acetylcholine
Correct, and both are used during surgery to produce complete muscle relaxation.
As structural analogues of norepinephrine acting at adrenergic receptors
They act at the cholinergic neuromuscular junction.
As enzymes that degrade acetylcholine at the endplate
That is acetylcholinesterase, not a drug class here.
As calcium channel blockers acting on the sarcoplasmic reticulum
That is dantrolene's territory.

E.q: A patient stops propranolol abruptly and develops arrhythmias. Why?
opts: Accumulated metabolite
Not the stated mechanism.
Withdrawal of the vehicle
Not a real mechanism.
Beta receptor up-regulation
Never stop a beta blocker suddenly.
Rebound alpha stimulation
Not the stated mechanism.

E.io: 4 — Predict the effects of adrenergic and cholinergic stimulation and inhibition on effector organs
E.q: Why are norepinephrine's actions diminished but not reversed by phenoxybenzamine?
opts: Norepinephrine is not bound by alpha receptors
It is chiefly an alpha agonist.
Norepinephrine is metabolised faster than epinephrine
Metabolism is not the explanation given.
Norepinephrine acts only on dopaminergic receptors
Those are dopamine's renal targets.
It lacks significant beta activity on vessels
Correct, so there is no vasodilating component left to unmask.

E.q: Aztreonam's spectrum is described as resembling which other class?
opts: Aminoglycosides
Correct. Both cover Gram-negatives including Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Enterobacteriaceae, with no Gram-positive or anaerobic activity.
Macrolides
Macrolides cover Gram-positive aerobes and atypicals, which is nearly the opposite profile.
Glycopeptides
Vancomycin covers Gram-positives only, the reverse of aztreonam.
Nitroimidazoles
Metronidazole covers anaerobes and parasites, which aztreonam does not touch.

E.io: 2 — Describe the molecular mechanism of action of dermatologic drugs
E.q: What happens to benzoyl peroxide after it penetrates the stratum corneum?
opts: It is converted to benzoic acid, which is active against Propionibacterium acnes
Correct. It crosses unchanged and is converted once through.
It is converted to salicylic acid, which is keratinolytic
Salicylic acid is a separate agent in the lecture with its own keratinolytic action.
It is converted to retinoic acid, which corrects keratinization
Retinoic acid is the acid form of vitamin A and belongs to the retinoid section.
It remains unchanged in the skin and works purely by oxidising sebum within the follicle
The lecture specifies conversion after penetration rather than an unchanged action.

E.io: 5 — Identify the location and effects of alpha-one, alpha-two, beta-one and beta-two stimulation
E.q: Which receptor does dobutamine selectively stimulate?
opts: Alpha-two
That is clonidine.
Beta-one
Correct, a synthetic selective agonist.
Beta-two
That is albuterol.
Alpha-one
That is phenylephrine.

E.io: 5 — Identify the location and effects of alpha-one, alpha-two, beta-one and beta-two stimulation
E.q: How does an alpha-two agonist such as clonidine lower blood pressure?
opts: It reduces central sympathetic outflow
Correct, so an agonist produces vasodilation by damping sympathetic drive.
It blocks alpha-one receptors on vascular smooth muscle
That is the prazosin group, which are antagonists.
It blocks beta-one receptors in the heart
That is a beta blocker.
It depletes vesicular norepinephrine
That is reserpine.

E.q: What is the echinocandin mechanism of action?
opts: Inhibits lanosterol demethylase, cutting ergosterol
That is the azole mechanism, acting on the membrane rather than the wall.
Formation of membrane channels allowing potassium to leak from the cell
That is amphotericin B.
Disruption of the mitotic spindle, halting cell division
That is griseofulvin.
Inhibits 1,3-beta-D-glucan synthase in the cell wall
Correct. Caspofungin, micafungin and anidulafungin are the three agents, and the wall target is unique among the antifungals here.

E.io: 9 — List commonly used protocols and patient monitoring for dermatologic drugs
E.q: An exacerbation needs a medium to high potency steroid. What next?
opts: Stop abruptly once the flare settles and use nothing further
The lecture steps down rather than stopping outright.
Add an oral corticosteroid for the same duration
Oral corticosteroids are a separate short-course option, not a routine addition.
Use it for one to two weeks, then switch to a lower potency
Correct. The step-down is the protocol rather than continuing at strength.
Continue it indefinitely to prevent relapse
Prolonged use at potency is what drives the adverse effects the lecture lists.

E.q: Which drug is used for chronic management of myasthenia gravis?
opts: Succinylcholine
A paralytic.
Pyridostigmine
Edrophonium is for diagnosis, not maintenance.
Edrophonium
Short-acting, used to diagnose.
Atropine
Would worsen weakness.

E.q: A patient asks how long griseofulvin takes for a toenail infection. What do you say?
opts: Up to 12 months
Scalp 1 month, fingernails 6 to 9, toenails up to 12.
About 2 weeks
Far too short.
About 6 weeks
That is closer to a fingernail course.
A single dose
That is fluconazole for vaginal candidiasis.

E.io: 10 — Outline appropriate patient education for dermatologic drugs
E.q: A patient on imiquimod has redness, swelling and erosions. What does this mean?
opts: Irritation in nearly all; inflammation parallels efficacy
Correct, so the reaction is expected and is not by itself a reason to stop.
It indicates an allergic reaction and the drug should be stopped
The lecture frames the inflammation as intrinsic to how the drug works.
It is unusual and suggests secondary bacterial infection
Irritation occurs in virtually all patients rather than being unusual.
The dose is too low; increase the frequency
The lecture does not tie the reaction to underdosing.

E.io: 3 — Classify the neurotransmitters released and the types of receptors found within the ANS
E.q: Which is the major inhibitory transmitter in the brain?
opts: Norepinephrine, which regulates normal brain processes
Norepinephrine is described as usually excitatory in normal brain processes.
Gamma-aminobutyric acid
Correct, while glycine is given as the inhibitory transmitter used by spinal cord neurons.
Glycine, the inhibitory transmitter of spinal cord neurons
Glycine is inhibitory but the lecture places it in the spinal cord rather than as the brain's major one.
Acetylcholine, which controls memory in brain neurons
Acetylcholine is described as usually excitatory.

E.q: Which herpesviruses are grouped as targets for antiviral therapy?
opts: Varicella-zoster and hepatitis B
Hepatitis is not covered here.
Herpes simplex, varicella-zoster and cytomegalovirus
Correct — the first two share the acyclovir family, while cytomegalovirus needs ganciclovir.
Herpes simplex and influenza A only
Influenza is not a herpesvirus and is treated with oseltamivir.
Cytomegalovirus and human immunodeficiency virus
Antiretroviral therapy is outside this lecture.

E.io: 2 — Describe the molecular mechanism of action of dermatologic drugs
E.q: What is the mechanism of the topical azole antifungals?
opts: They inhibit fungal cytochrome P450, preventing cell wall formation
Correct, and the named agents are clotrimazole, ketoconazole, miconazole and sertaconazole.
They inhibit ergosterol production directly
That is how the lecture describes the allylamines.
They inhibit uptake of molecular precursors at the fungal cell wall
That is ciclopirox.
They bind fungal transfer RNA to stop protein synthesis
No antifungal in the lecture works this way.

E.q: A patient on intravenous acyclovir has a rising creatinine. What prevents this?
opts: Good hydration
It crystallizes in the renal tubule.
A loop diuretic
Not the stated measure.
Alkalinising the urine
Not the stated measure.
Slowing the infusion
Hydration is the measure given.

E.q: What is the mechanism of the benzimidazoles albendazole and mebendazole?
opts: Block helminth microtubules and glucose uptake
Correct. Note this content is taught in the deck but sits outside the syllabus objectives, which name only antibacterials, antivirals and antifungals.
Release acetylcholine and block cholinesterase
That is pyrantel pamoate's mechanism.
They inhibit ergosterol synthesis in the helminth membrane
Ergosterol is a fungal target; helminths are not addressed that way here.
They interact with parasite DNA to cause strand breakage
That describes metronidazole's action.

E.q: A patient using triple antibiotic ointment develops dermatitis around the wound. Which component?
opts: The petrolatum base
Not the flagged sensitiser.
Neomycin
It frequently causes sensitization.
Bacitracin
Allergic dermatitis is rare and there is no systemic toxicity.
Polymyxin B
Allergic reactions are uncommon.

E.q: Which antiviral does NOT act on viral nucleic acid?
opts: Ganciclovir, which inhibits in a manner similar to acyclovir
Ganciclovir acts on nucleic acid like acyclovir.
Penciclovir, which has a mechanism similar to acyclovir
Penciclovir also acts on viral nucleic acid.
Oseltamivir, which inhibits neuraminidase to block viral release
Correct. The guanine analogues all terminate the nucleic acid chain; oseltamivir works at a completely different stage.
Acyclovir, which is incorporated into viral DNA
Acyclovir does act on nucleic acid, by chain termination.

E.q: A transplant recipient develops cytomegalovirus retinitis. Why is acyclovir not the answer?
opts: Acyclovir is intravenous only and unsafe in transplant
Acyclovir is available orally, and transplant status is not a contraindication to it.
Acyclovir causes neutropenia in a third of patients
That poor tolerability belongs to intravenous ganciclovir.
Acyclovir has no antiviral activity at all in immunocompromised patients
It retains activity; it simply does not cover cytomegalovirus.
Acyclovir for simplex and zoster; ganciclovir for CMV
Correct. All are guanine analogues, but the indications are drawn along virus lines rather than by drug family.

E.q: Which renal adverse effect is characteristic of acyclovir, and how is it mitigated?
opts: It causes interstitial nephritis requiring corticosteroids
Interstitial nephritis is listed among the aminopenicillin effects.
Its intravenous vehicle accumulates in renal failure
That is voriconazole's cyclodextrin problem.
It crystallises in the renal tubule, so hydration and renal function must be maintained
Correct. Note how this differs from amphotericin B, which damages the tubule directly rather than crystallising in it.
It causes direct renal tubule damage requiring hydration with normal saline
That is amphotericin B's mechanism of renal injury.

E.io: 2 — Common modes of action of antimicrobial agents
E.q: Which antifungal target exists in the fungal cell wall and has no mammalian counterpart?
opts: Ergosterol, which the polyenes bind
Ergosterol sits in the membrane, and mammalian membranes contain the related sterol cholesterol.
Lanosterol demethylase, which the azole agents inhibit
That is a cytochrome P450 enzyme with human counterparts, which is exactly why azoles cause interactions.
Microtubules, which griseofulvin disrupts
Mammalian cells have microtubules too.
1,3-beta-D-glucan, whose synthase the echinocandins inhibit
Correct. Mammalian cells have no cell wall at all, which makes this the cleanest selective target among the antifungals.

E.io: 10 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic agonists
E.q: What happened to ephedra-containing herbal products?
opts: They were banned in 2004
Correct.
They were moved behind the pharmacy counter
That was pseudoephedrine.
They were reclassified as prescription only
Not what the lecture states.
They remain freely available
They were banned.

E.q: Which adverse effects and interactions accompany griseofulvin?
opts: Nephrotoxicity and electrolyte wasting
Those belong to amphotericin B.
Visual disturbance in 30 percent with hepatic and renal effects
That profile is voriconazole's.
Headache, confusion, fatigue and blurred vision
Correct. Note it induces enzymes where the azoles inhibit them — opposite directions of interaction within the same broad category of drug.
CYP3A4 inhibition, raising substrate levels
Griseofulvin induces rather than inhibits, which pushes substrate levels the other way.

E.q: Which carbapenem lacks Pseudomonas aeruginosa coverage?
opts: Doripenem
Doripenem retains antipseudomonal activity.
Ertapenem
Correct. The class covers Pseudomonas as a rule, and ertapenem is the stated exception.
Meropenem
Meropenem retains antipseudomonal activity.
Imipenem
Imipenem retains antipseudomonal activity.

E.io: 10 — Outline appropriate patient education for dermatologic drugs
E.q: A patient is starting a topical azole. How long is the course?
opts: Treatment is generally prolonged, on the order of two to three weeks
Correct, and stopping early is how a treated infection returns.
A single application is usually curative
The lecture describes prolonged treatment rather than single dosing.
Treatment continues until the rash disappears, then stops immediately
The lecture frames the course by duration rather than by appearance alone.
Treatment must continue for at least six months
That is far longer than the lecture states.

E.io: 1 — Identify dermatologic drug classes and commonly prescribed dermatologic drugs
E.q: Which topical antibiotic is preferred for acne, and what is happening to the alternative?
opts: Neomycin is preferred; polymyxin B is losing efficacy
Neomycin is noted for causing sensitisation and is not the acne agent.
Clindamycin preferred; erythromycin losing efficacy
Correct, and both are noted to lack systemic side effects.
Erythromycin is preferred; clindamycin is losing efficacy to resistance
This reverses the lecture's position.
Mupirocin preferred; bacitracin losing efficacy
Those two belong to the other topical antibiotics section, not to acne.

E.q: A patient on an SSRI is started on linezolid and becomes agitated, febrile and tremulous. What is this?
opts: Sepsis
The drug interaction is the point.
Serotonin syndrome
Interacts with SSRIs, tyramine foods and pseudoephedrine.
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Not the interaction being tested.
Malignant hyperthermia
That follows succinylcholine with halothane.

E.io: 10 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic agonists
E.q: Why is pseudoephedrine kept behind the pharmacy counter?
opts: It causes rebound congestion after three days
That is oxymetazoline.
It requires blood pressure monitoring
Not the reason the lecture gives.
It was banned by the Food and Drug Administration
It was ephedra-containing herbal products that were banned in 2004.
It can be converted to methamphetamine
Correct, which is a regulatory rather than a pharmacological reason.

E.q: Once phosphorylated and incorporated into viral DNA, how does acyclovir stop replication?
opts: It inhibits DNA gyrase and prevents supercoiling
That is the fluoroquinolone mechanism in bacteria.
It is a guanine analogue lacking the sugar moiety, so the chain cannot elongate past it
Correct — chain termination by a missing sugar, which is a structural rather than an enzymatic block.
It cross-links the two strands of viral DNA so that they can no longer separate
Cross-linking is not the mechanism described.
It causes helical structure loss and strand breakage
That is metronidazole's effect on bacterial DNA.

E.q: How should griseofulvin be taken to improve absorption?
opts: With milk
Not the stated advice.
With an antacid
Not the stated advice.
With a high-fat meal
Absorption increases with fat.
On an empty stomach
The opposite of the advice.

E.q: Which organisms is amphotericin B indicated against?
opts: Helminths including hookworm and pinworm
Those are the anthelmintic targets.
Influenza A and B
That is oseltamivir's target and is viral rather than fungal.
The systemic mycoses; Aspergillus if invasive
Correct. Its breadth is why it remained the reference agent until voriconazole displaced it for aspergillosis.
Dermatophytes of skin, hair and nails only
Those are treated by griseofulvin and the allylamines; amphotericin B is a systemic agent.

E.io: 3 — Identify indications for commonly used dermatologic drugs
E.q: Which gap in coverage does tolnaftate have?
opts: It has no activity on the scalp
Site is not the stated gap.
It has no Candida activity
Correct, and nystatin is the agent the lecture pairs with candidal infection.
It has no dermatophyte activity
Dermatophyte infection is what it is used for.
It has no activity below the stratum corneum
This is not the limitation the lecture gives.

E.io: 6 — Summarize the synthesis, release, and subsequent destiny of ANS neurotransmitters
E.q: Why do the noncatecholamines have longer half-lives?
opts: They are not substrates for the inactivating enzymes
Correct, and their greater lipid solubility also increases central penetration.
They are protein bound and released slowly from plasma
Protein binding is not the reason the lecture gives.
They are stored in vesicles and released over hours
Storage is not what determines their duration here.
They are excreted unchanged by the kidney
Renal handling is not the stated reason.

E.q: How does pyrantel pamoate kill its target parasites?
opts: It blocks neuraminidase and prevents the parasite from leaving host cells
Neuraminidase inhibition is oseltamivir's antiviral mechanism.
Releases acetylcholine and blocks cholinesterase
Correct, and it is used for pinworm and hookworm.
It inhibits formation of helminth microtubules and blocks glucose uptake
That is the benzimidazole mechanism.
Inhibits squalene epoxidase, depleting ergosterol
That is an antifungal mechanism and does not apply.

E.q: Which adverse effects are listed for posaconazole?
opts: QT prolongation, fever, diarrhoea, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and thrombocytopenia
Correct. The QT effect places it alongside the macrolides and fluoroquinolones as a drug to watch in combination.
Visual disturbance in about 30 percent of patients
That is voriconazole's characteristic effect.
Headache in about 15 percent of patients, with mental confusion and blurred vision
That profile belongs to griseofulvin.
Bone marrow suppression and hepatotoxicity
Those are flucytosine's effects.

E.io: 3 — Classify the neurotransmitters released and the types of receptors found within the ANS
E.q: What are the three general types of signalling between cells?
opts: Neurotransmitters, receptors and second messengers
Receptors and second messengers are parts of the response, not types of signal.
Afferent, efferent and enteric signalling
Those are anatomical divisions rather than signalling types.
Hormones, local mediators and neurotransmitters
Correct, and the neurotransmitters of interest here are acetylcholine, norepinephrine and epinephrine.
Hormones, enzymes and ion channels
Enzymes and channels are effectors rather than signalling categories here.

E.io: 7 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: cholinergic agonists
E.q: Why is succinylcholine suited to rapid sequence intubation?
opts: Its long duration, which covers the whole procedure
The duration is extremely short.
Its lack of any cardiovascular effect
It initially produces fasciculations and a ganglionic block.
Its reversibility with neostigmine
Reversal with an anticholinesterase applies to the nondepolarizing agents.
Its rapid onset and short duration of action
Correct, with the short duration owing to rapid breakdown by plasma enzyme.

E.io: 7 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: cholinergic agonists
E.q: What distinguishes scopolamine from atropine?
opts: It has no central effects and acts purely peripherally
Its peripheral effects resemble atropine's, but the central action is what sets it apart.
It stimulates muscarinic receptors rather than blocking them
It is an antimuscarinic.
It is a selective bladder agent
Those are the synthetic agents such as oxybutynin and tolterodine.
Greater central action, preventing motion sickness
Correct, with sedation at lower doses and excitement at higher ones.

E.q: Which organism defeats the penicillinase-resistant penicillins, and what replaces them?
opts: Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus, for which linezolid is the treatment of choice
Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus is a separate problem addressed by linezolid and daptomycin.
Extended-spectrum beta-lactamase producing organisms, for which carbapenems are preferred
Those organisms are a Gram-negative problem; this class never covered them.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa, for which cefepime is preferred
Pseudomonas was never within this class's spectrum.
MRSA, for which vancomycin is the treatment of choice
Correct. The class was built for Staphylococcus aureus and methicillin resistance is precisely what defeats it.

E.q: Which amphotericin B formulation is the conventional, non-lipid one?
opts: Amphotericin B lipid complex, marketed as Abelcet
That is one of the lipid formulations developed to reduce toxicity.
Liposomal amphotericin B, marketed as AmBisome
That is the liposomal lipid formulation.
Amphotericin B colloidal suspension, marketed as Amphotec
That is the colloidal lipid formulation.
Amphotericin B deoxycholate, marketed as Fungizone
Correct. The three lipid alternatives are the lipid complex, the colloidal suspension and the liposomal form.

E.io: 11 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic antagonists
E.q: Which hypertensive crisis is phentolamine used for?
opts: Crisis in thyroid storm
Propranolol is the agent linked to hyperthyroidism.
Abrupt clonidine withdrawal
Correct, which is the rebound the clonidine slide warns about.
Crisis in pre-eclampsia
Not an indication given.
Crisis from cocaine intoxication
Not the indication the lecture names.

E.io: 3 — Classify the neurotransmitters released and the types of receptors found within the ANS
E.q: Which muscarinic receptor subtypes are functionally characterised?
opts: M1 and M2 only
M3 is also functionally characterised, on bladder, exocrine glands and smooth muscle.
M2 and M4 only, the cardiac subtypes
M2 is the cardiac one, but M4 is listed only as neuronal.
M1, M2 and M3 only, of five subclasses
Correct. M4 and M5 are listed as neuronal without further characterisation.
All five subclasses, M1 through M5
The lecture limits functional characterisation to the first three.

E.q: What is the allylamine mechanism of action?
opts: Inhibition of glucan synthesis in the cell wall
That is the echinocandin mechanism.
Inhibition of squalene epoxidase, reducing ergosterol synthesis
Correct. Same end point as the azoles, reached at an earlier step of the pathway.
Inhibition of lanosterol demethylase, reducing ergosterol synthesis
That is where the azoles act.
Binding ergosterol already present and forming membrane channels
That is the polyene mechanism.

E.q: Which indications are given for cefazolin?
opts: Meningitis and neonatal sepsis
Ceftriaxone and cefotaxime are the agents named for central nervous system and neonatal indications.
Complicated intra-abdominal and anaerobic infection
That requires anaerobic coverage the first generation does not provide.
Surgical prophylaxis, MSSA and urinary tract infection
Correct. Cephalexin covers a similar niche orally, aimed at cellulitis and urinary tract infection.
Neutropenic fever and hospital-acquired pneumonia
Those indications belong to cefepime, the fourth generation agent.

E.io: 7 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: cholinergic agonists
E.q: Which agents treat Alzheimer disease, and why?
opts: Atropine, scopolamine and glycopyrrolate, because they reduce secretions
Those are antimuscarinics and would worsen a cholinergic deficiency.
Pralidoxime and dantrolene, because they restore enzyme function
Those are antidotes for anticholinesterase poisoning and malignant hyperthermia.
Donepezil, rivastigmine and galantamine
Correct, and their common adverse effect is gastrointestinal distress.
Physostigmine, neostigmine and pyridostigmine, because they cross into the brain
Those are used for anticholinergic overdose and myasthenia gravis.

E.q: What warning applies to polymyxin B?
opts: Avoid in pregnancy; absorption through inflamed skin
Pregnancy contraindications in this lecture attach to the retinoids and tetracyclines.
Avoid it in children under eight because it stains teeth
That restriction belongs to the tetracyclines.
Avoid it with benzoyl peroxide because it is inactivated
That interaction is tretinoin with benzoyl peroxide.
Not on open wounds in high doses; neuro and nephrotoxicity
Correct. Loss of the barrier is what turns a topical agent into a systemic exposure.

E.io: 4 — Predict the effects of adrenergic and cholinergic stimulation and inhibition on effector organs
E.q: How does atropine's cardiovascular effect vary with dose?
opts: Tachycardia at lower doses and bradycardia at higher doses
This reverses the relationship.
Bradycardia at every dose
The effect is dose-dependent in both directions.
No cardiac effect, since its action is confined to secretions
Its cardiac use is explicit in the lecture.
Bradycardia at lower doses and tachycardia at higher doses
Correct, and it is given during a code to treat bradycardia.

E.q: How do levofloxacin and moxifloxacin differ in coverage?
opts: Levofloxacin covers atypicals; moxifloxacin does not
Both are described as covering Streptococcus pneumoniae and atypicals.
Moxifloxacin requires renal adjustment; levofloxacin does not
The reverse is stated — moxifloxacin has no dosing consideration listed while levofloxacin is renally adjusted.
Levofloxacin has Pseudomonas coverage; moxifloxacin does not
Correct. Both improve on ciprofloxacin's Gram-positive activity and both cover community-acquired pneumonia.
Moxifloxacin has Pseudomonas coverage; levofloxacin does not
This reverses the two agents.

E.q: Which beta-lactamase inhibitor is paired with piperacillin?
opts: Sulbactam, marketed as Unasyn
Sulbactam is the partner for ampicillin, not piperacillin.
Clavulanate, marketed as Augmentin
Clavulanate is combined with amoxicillin in Augmentin.
Avibactam, marketed as Avycaz
That pairing is not covered in this lecture's list of three inhibitors.
Tazobactam, marketed as Zosyn
Correct. Sulbactam pairs with ampicillin as Unasyn, and clavulanate with amoxicillin as Augmentin.

E.q: Linezolid is the drug of choice for which infections, and what does it not cover?
opts: Anaerobic intra-abdominal infection; it does not cover aerobes
Anaerobes are explicitly outside its coverage.
Atypical pneumonia; it does not cover Staphylococcus
Staphylococcus, including resistant strains, is precisely what it is for.
Hospital and community MRSA, with no Gram-negative cover
Correct. It also covers multidrug-resistant pneumococcus and vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus.
Pseudomonal and resistant Gram-negative infection only
This inverts the spectrum entirely.

E.q: How does vancomycin inhibit cell wall synthesis, and how does this differ from a penicillin?
opts: It inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit and blocks transpeptidation
Vancomycin is not a protein synthesis inhibitor, and the lecture notes it is not a beta-lactam.
It disrupts the outer membrane by displacing magnesium and calcium ions
That is the polymyxin detergent mechanism.
Binds the D-alanine residues to block cross-linking
Correct. Penicillin mimics the substrate and disables the enzyme; vancomycin covers the substrate itself, which is why resistance is harder to develop.
Covalently inactivates the penicillin-binding protein
That is the penicillin mechanism; vancomycin binds the substrate, not the enzyme.

E.io: 5 — Summarize side effects and toxic manifestations of dermatologic drugs
E.q: Which systemic effects do topical corticosteroids cause?
opts: Hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity
Neuro and nephrotoxicity are raised for polymyxin B on denuded skin, not for steroids.
Raised serum lipids and brittle nails
Those belong to systemic isotretinoin.
Photosensitivity, sunburn, desquamation and stinging
That is the topical retinoid profile.
Adrenal suppression, hyperglycaemia, glaucoma, cataracts
Correct. That a topical agent can do all of this is the point of the potency and duration warnings.

E.io: 8 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: cholinergic antagonists
E.q: Which muscles does a nondepolarizing blocker paralyse first?
opts: The small muscles of the face and eye
Correct, and the diaphragm goes last, with recovery in reverse order.
The diaphragm and intercostal muscles
Those are last to be affected, which is what makes the sequence survivable.
The muscles of the trunk and neck
Those come partway through the sequence.
All skeletal muscle simultaneously
The lecture is explicit that sensitivity varies.

E.q: A child needs a topical steroid for facial eczema. Which potency?
opts: Any potency is fine
Site determines potency.
Low potency
Low potency for face, intertriginous areas and infants.
Superpotent
Inappropriate for the face.
High potency
Inappropriate for the face.

E.q: Within what window must oseltamivir be started?
opts: At any point during the illness, with equal benefit
Timing is central to its effectiveness.
As soon as possible, within 48 hours of symptom onset
Correct. Because it blocks release rather than killing virus already present, late treatment has little to act on.
Within 7 days of symptom onset
The stated window is considerably shorter.
Within the first 24 hours, as with acyclovir in chickenpox
The 24-hour figure belongs to acyclovir in chickenpox; oseltamivir's window is 48 hours.

E.io: 10 — Mechanism, pharmacokinetics, indications, contraindications and adverse effects: adrenergic agonists
E.q: What are dopamine's adverse effects?
opts: Tremor, restlessness and anxiety
Those are albuterol's.
Sedation and dry mouth
Those are clonidine's.
Bronchoconstriction
That is a beta blocker effect.
Nausea, hypertension and arrhythmias
Correct.

E.io: 4 — Predict the effects of adrenergic and cholinergic stimulation and inhibition on effector organs
E.q: What is the risk of stopping clonidine abruptly?
opts: Rebound bronchospasm
That risk belongs to the beta agonists and blockers.
Adrenal suppression
That belongs to corticosteroids.
Rebound nasal congestion
That is oxymetazoline.
Rebound hypertension
Correct, which is why it is tapered rather than stopped.

E.q: Clindamycin is the drug of choice for which situations?
opts: Toxin-mediated disease, skin, bone, penicillin allergy
Correct. The toxin-mediated indication follows from inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis and therefore toxin production.
Pseudomonal pneumonia and febrile neutropenia
It has no Gram-negative aerobic coverage at all.
Urinary tract infection and pyelonephritis
Urinary indications belong to agents with Gram-negative coverage.
Meningitis, cerebral abscess and neurosurgical prophylaxis
Central nervous system penetration is discussed for carbapenems and third generation cephalosporins.
